# DevOps Lounge: full text

> DevOps Lounge is a free Discord community for developers and DevOps engineers at every level. Join: https://discord.gg/XHtBz8rZp5. Website: https://sabbagh-moh.github.io/devops-lounge/

## About
Members ask programming questions in forums with solved tags, get code reviews, share projects in a showroom with upvotes, and find collaborators. There are ten tracks and rooms in English, Arabic, Spanish, Portuguese, French and Russian. A bot trap, raid protection and AutoMod keep spam out.

### What is DevOps Lounge?
A free Discord community for developers and DevOps engineers at every level. Members ask questions, share projects, review code and find people to build with.

### Is it free?
Yes. Joining is free and there is nothing to buy.

### I am just starting out. Is it for me?
Yes. There is a beginner track and a beginner corner, and every help forum welcomes first questions. Experienced engineers are there too, which is what makes the answers good.

### What languages can I talk in?
English is shared by everyone, and there are rooms in Arabic, Spanish, Portuguese, French and Russian.

### What topics does it cover?
Ten tracks: AI, web, app development, frontend, backend, mobile, data and ML, security, DevOps and cloud, and game development, plus career and interview help.

### How do I get help with my code?
Post in the ask-a-question forum with what you tried and the error you see. When it is solved, the thread is tagged so others can find the answer later. There is also a code review forum.

## Free developer tools (run in the browser, nothing uploaded)
### Prompt Builder
URL: https://sabbagh-moh.github.io/devops-lounge/tools/prompt-builder/
Write your idea the way you would say it, like "a store like Gymshark". The builder works out what you want, adds the pages, stack, references and quality bar an expert would, and for images the film look, light and lens.
- It understands the request: It tells a project from code, a bug, a review, a question or an image, and recognizes 14 kinds of projects, 27 well-known products as references, 13 design styles, 15 languages and 41 frameworks and services.
- It adds what experts add: For a project: the pages and features that kind of product needs, a stack, a quality bar and the questions to answer first. For a reference like Gymshark: what to borrow, and a reminder not to copy the brand.
- Images get a real look: Your mood words become a film or cinematographer reference, light, lens, color and film stock, written in the syntax of Midjourney, Stable Diffusion, Flux or ChatGPT.
- Q: Does it use AI? A: No. It runs a set of rules in your browser, so it is instant, free and private. Use the prompt it builds with any AI assistant you like.
- Q: Which image models does it support? A: Midjourney (with --ar and --no), Stable Diffusion (with a negative prompt), Flux and ChatGPT image generation.
- Q: Is my idea sent anywhere? A: No. Everything happens on this page. Nothing is uploaded or stored.

### Token Counter
URL: https://sabbagh-moh.github.io/devops-lounge/tools/token-counter/
Paste a prompt, a document or code. See roughly how many tokens it uses, whether it fits common context windows, and what it costs to send.
- An honest estimate: Common English words are one token, long words several, and Arabic, Russian and Chinese text use more tokens per character. The range covers how real tokenizers differ.
- Context windows: The bars show how much of each common window size your text fills, before the model writes a word back.
- Cost: Enter your model's current input price to see what one request costs. Prices change, so take them from your provider.
- Q: Is this exact? A: It is an estimate, usually within 10 to 15 percent. Exact counts need the model's own tokenizer, and every model family has a different one.
- Q: Why does Arabic use more tokens? A: Tokenizers are trained mostly on English, so other scripts get split into smaller pieces.
- Q: Is my text sent anywhere? A: No. Counting happens in your browser.
Rules of thumb:
- 1 token : 4 characters of English, or about 3/4 of a word
- 100 tokens : About 75 English words
- 1,000 words of English : About 1,300 tokens
- A page of code : About 500 to 800 tokens
- Arabic or Russian text : Often 1.5 to 3 times the tokens of the same length in English

### AI Tool Schema Builder
URL: https://sabbagh-moh.github.io/devops-lounge/tools/tool-schema/
Describe a tool and its parameters once. Get the exact JSON that OpenAI function calling, Claude tool use and MCP servers expect, with tips that help the model call it right.
- One definition, three formats: OpenAI wraps the schema in a function object, Claude calls it input_schema, and MCP calls it inputSchema. The parameters are the same JSON Schema.
- Strict mode: When every parameter is required, the OpenAI version turns on strict mode so the model must follow the schema exactly.
- Descriptions matter: Models choose tools and fill values from the descriptions. The tips point out anything vague.
- Q: Can I make a parameter optional? A: Untick Required. It stays in the properties but leaves the required list.
- Q: Where do I put this? A: In the tools list of your API request, or in the tools your MCP server lists.

### JSON to TypeScript
URL: https://sabbagh-moh.github.io/devops-lounge/tools/json-to-types/
Paste an API response or any JSON example. Get TypeScript interfaces, a Zod schema or a JSON Schema, with optional fields worked out from arrays.
- Merged arrays: Every item in an array is read, so a field that only some items have becomes optional, and mixed types become unions.
- Named types: Nested objects get their own interfaces, named after their keys. Array items are named in the singular.
- Q: Does it handle dates? A: JSON has no date type, so dates come out as strings. Add z.string().datetime() in Zod if you want them checked.
- Q: Is my JSON uploaded? A: No. It is converted in your browser.

### cURL Converter
URL: https://sabbagh-moh.github.io/devops-lounge/tools/curl-converter/
Paste a cURL command from API docs or your browser's network tab. Get clean fetch, axios or Python requests code with headers, body and auth carried over.
- Understands the usual flags: -X, -H, -d and its variants, --json, -u for basic auth, -b for cookies, -G for query strings, and line breaks with backslashes.
- JSON stays JSON: A JSON body becomes a real object in the code, so you can edit it easily.
- Q: Where do I get a cURL command? A: In Chrome or Edge, open the Network tab, right-click a request and choose Copy as cURL.
- Q: Are my tokens safe? A: The command never leaves your browser. Still, replace real tokens before you share code.
cURL flags it understands:
- -X, --request : HTTP method, like POST or DELETE
- -H, --header : A request header
- -d, --data, --data-raw : Request body
- --json : JSON body, with JSON headers set
- -u, --user : Basic auth, turned into an Authorization header
- -b, --cookie : Cookies
- -G, --get : Send the data as a query string
- -A, --user-agent : The User-Agent header

### Text Diff
URL: https://sabbagh-moh.github.io/devops-lounge/tools/diff/
Paste two versions of a file, a config or any text. Added and removed lines are marked with their line numbers.
- Line by line: It finds the longest run of lines the two texts share, then marks everything else as added or removed.
- Whitespace: Turn on Ignore whitespace to skip changes that are only indentation or spacing.
- Q: How long can the texts be? A: A few thousand lines each works well. Much longer files are better compared with git diff.
- Q: Is my text uploaded? A: No. The comparison runs in your browser.

### Color and Contrast
URL: https://sabbagh-moh.github.io/devops-lounge/tools/color-contrast/
Type any color to get HEX, RGB, HSL and OKLCH, check its contrast against a background for WCAG, and pick a lighter or darker shade.
- Any format in: Names like navy, hex, rgb(), hsl(), oklch() and more are read by your browser's own color engine.
- WCAG levels: Body text needs 4.5:1 for AA and 7:1 for AAA. Large or bold text needs 3:1 for AA.
- Q: What is OKLCH? A: A color format where lightness matches how bright colors look to people, which makes building palettes easier.
- Q: Which level should I aim for? A: AA for everything, and AAA for long reading text when you can.

### Cron Builder
URL: https://sabbagh-moh.github.io/devops-lounge/tools/cron/
Type a cron expression or build one field by field. It is explained in plain words, with the next five run times in your time zone.
- Five fields: Minute, hour, day of month, month and day of week. Use * for any value, */n for every n, a-b for a range and commas for lists.
- Names work too: MON-FRI and JAN-DEC are understood, and so are @daily, @hourly and @weekly.
- The day rule: When both day fields are set, cron runs when either one matches. The next-run list follows that rule.
- Q: What does */5 mean? A: Every 5 units of that field. In the minute field, */5 runs at minutes 0, 5, 10 and so on.
- Q: Is Sunday 0 or 7? A: Both. Cron accepts 0 and 7 for Sunday.
- Q: Which time zone is used? A: Your browser's. Servers often run cron in UTC, so check your server's time zone too.
Common cron schedules:
- * * * * * : Every minute
- */5 * * * * : Every 5 minutes
- */15 * * * * : Every 15 minutes
- 0 * * * * : Every hour, on the hour
- 0 */6 * * * : Every 6 hours
- 0 0 * * * : Every day at midnight
- 0 9 * * * : Every day at 09:00
- 30 18 * * 1-5 : Weekdays at 18:30
- 0 9 * * 1 : Every Monday at 09:00
- 0 0 * * 0 : Every Sunday at midnight
- 0 0 1 * * : The first day of every month
- 0 0 1 1 * : Once a year, on 1 January

### Regex Tester
URL: https://sabbagh-moh.github.io/devops-lounge/tools/regex/
Write a pattern, paste some text, and every match lights up as you type, with the captured groups listed below.
- JavaScript flavor: Patterns run with the JavaScript engine in your browser, the same one Node.js uses.
- Flags: g finds every match, i ignores case, m makes ^ and $ work per line, s lets . match new lines, u enables full Unicode.
- Groups: Parentheses capture parts of a match. They are listed as $1, $2 and so on.
- Q: Why does my pattern work here but not in Python? A: Regex flavors differ a little. Lookbehind, named groups and some escapes are written differently in Python, PCRE and JavaScript.
- Q: Is my text sent anywhere? A: No. Matching happens in your browser.
Patterns developers use every day:
- Email address (practical) : [\w.+-]+@[\w-]+\.[\w.-]+
- URL : https?:\/\/[^\s]+
- IPv4 address : \b(?:\d{1,3}\.){3}\d{1,3}\b
- Date (YYYY-MM-DD) : \d{4}-\d{2}-\d{2}
- Time (HH:MM, 24h) : ([01]\d|2[0-3]):[0-5]\d
- Hex color : #(?:[0-9a-fA-F]{3}){1,2}\b
- UUID : [0-9a-f]{8}-[0-9a-f]{4}-[0-9a-f]{4}-[0-9a-f]{4}-[0-9a-f]{12}
- URL slug : ^[a-z0-9]+(?:-[a-z0-9]+)*$
- Phone, international (E.164) : ^\+[1-9]\d{7,14}$
- Only digits : ^\d+$
- Leading and trailing spaces : ^\s+|\s+$

### JSON Formatter
URL: https://sabbagh-moh.github.io/devops-lounge/tools/json/
Paste JSON to format it, check that it is valid, sort the keys or minify it. Errors point to the line and column.
- Strict JSON: Keys need double quotes, and trailing commas and comments are not allowed. That is what APIs expect.
- Exact errors: When the JSON is broken, the line and column of the problem are shown.
- Q: Is there a size limit? A: Only your browser's memory. Files of several megabytes work fine.
- Q: Is my data uploaded? A: No. It never leaves this page.

### JWT Decoder
URL: https://sabbagh-moh.github.io/devops-lounge/tools/jwt/
Paste a token to read its header and payload, and see when it was issued and when it expires.
- Decoded, not verified: The header and payload are only Base64URL-encoded, so anyone can read them. Checking the signature needs the key.
- Never paste secrets: Tokens from production give access. Decode them here, where nothing is sent anywhere, then rotate any token you shared by mistake.
- Q: Can you verify the signature? A: Not here on purpose. Verifying needs your secret or public key, and a key should never be pasted into a website.
- Q: Why does my token show as expired? A: The exp claim is in Unix seconds. If it is in the past, servers reject the token.

### Timestamp Converter
URL: https://sabbagh-moh.github.io/devops-lounge/tools/timestamp/
Paste a Unix timestamp in seconds or milliseconds, or any date, and get every format you need.
- Seconds or milliseconds: Ten digits are read as seconds and thirteen as milliseconds, which is what JavaScript uses.
- Any date: Dates like 2026-11-11 14:30 or ISO strings with a time zone also work.
- Q: What is Unix time? A: The number of seconds since 1 January 1970 at midnight UTC. Most systems store time this way.
- Q: Why is my date off by some hours? A: Time zones. The ISO line shows UTC, and the next line shows your local time.

### Base64 and URL Encoder
URL: https://sabbagh-moh.github.io/devops-lounge/tools/base64/
Encode or decode Base64 and URL text. Arabic, emoji and every other character are handled correctly.
- UTF-8 first: Text is turned into UTF-8 bytes before encoding, so non-English text and emoji survive the round trip.
- URL-safe Base64: Decoding also accepts the URL-safe alphabet with - and _.
- Q: Is Base64 encryption? A: No. It only changes how bytes are written. Anyone can decode it.
- Q: When do I URL-encode? A: When a value goes inside a URL, like a search query, so characters like & and spaces do not break it.

### Password and UUID Generator
URL: https://sabbagh-moh.github.io/devops-lounge/tools/password/
Strong passwords and v4 UUIDs, made with your browser's secure random generator. Nothing is sent or saved.
- Real randomness: It uses crypto.getRandomValues, the same source browsers use for encryption, with no bias between characters.
- No look-alikes: Characters that are easy to confuse, like l, 1, O and 0, are left out.
- Q: How long should a password be? A: At least 16 characters for accounts that matter, and use a password manager so you never retype it.
- Q: Are the UUIDs unique? A: v4 UUIDs have 122 random bits, so a clash is practically impossible.

### chmod Calculator
URL: https://sabbagh-moh.github.io/devops-lounge/tools/chmod/
Tick who can read, write and run a file. You get the number, the letters and the command to paste.
- Three digits: One each for the owner, the group and everyone else. Read is 4, write is 2 and run is 1, added together.
- Common picks: 644 for normal files, 755 for scripts and folders, 600 for SSH keys.
- Q: What does 777 do? A: It lets anyone read, change and run the file. It is almost never what you want on a server.
- Q: Why does SSH refuse my key? A: Private keys must not be readable by others. Run chmod 600 on the key file.
Common permissions:
- 644 : -rw-r--r-- : Normal files: you edit, everyone reads
- 755 : -rwxr-xr-x : Scripts, programs and folders
- 600 : -rw------- : SSH private keys and secrets
- 700 : -rwx------ : Private folders like ~/.ssh
- 640 : -rw-r----- : Config files your group needs to read
- 775 : -rwxrwxr-x : Shared project folders
- 444 : -r--r--r-- : Files nobody should change
- 777 : -rwxrwxrwx : Almost never: anyone can change it

## The Vault: 249 hand-picked resources
### AI for developers
Hand-picked talks, papers, courses and tools for building with large language models, from your first prompt to agents in production. Each one comes with a short note on why it is worth your time.
- Intro to Large Language Models: Karpathy's one-hour talk (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=zjkBMFhNj_g): A single free talk that explains an LLM as an artifact (a big parameter file plus a small program that runs it), how training and fine-tuning produce one, and where the security problems come from. Start here if you use models daily but have never looked inside.
- The Illustrated Transformer (https://jalammar.github.io/illustrated-transformer/): Jay Alammar's diagram-driven walkthrough of the architecture from the original transformer paper: self-attention, multi-head attention, positional encoding and the encoder and decoder stacks. Read it before the paper, then keep it open next to the paper.
- Attention Is All You Need, the original transformer paper (https://arxiv.org/abs/1706.03762): The 2017 paper that introduced the transformer and dropped recurrence in favour of attention. Dense in places, but short, and nearly every modern language model descends from it. Pair it with the illustrated walkthrough.
- Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks (https://arxiv.org/abs/2005.11401): The paper that named RAG: a generator combined with a dense vector index over Wikipedia, trained together. Useful for understanding what the acronym originally meant before it became a catch-all for "put documents in the prompt".
- Hugging Face LLM Course (https://huggingface.co/learn/llm-course/chapter1/1): A free, hands-on course on using and fine-tuning transformer models with the Hugging Face libraries. Good first stop if you want to move from calling an API to understanding tokenizers, models and training loops.
- Hugging Face Agents Course (https://huggingface.co/learn/agents-course/unit0/introduction): A free course on building, running and evaluating AI agents, with practical units rather than only theory. Reach for it when you want a structured path into agents instead of piecing blog posts together.
- Practical Deep Learning for Coders (fast.ai) (https://course.fast.ai/): A free, code-first course that teaches deep learning top-down: you build working models early and learn the theory underneath as you go. A strong fit for developers who learn by running things.
- Neural Networks: Zero to Hero (https://karpathy.ai/zero-to-hero.html): Free video series by Andrej Karpathy that builds from backpropagation by hand up to a GPT-style language model in code. Slow and rewarding: the best way to make the maths feel concrete if you are willing to type along.
- Generative AI for Beginners from Microsoft (https://github.com/microsoft/generative-ai-for-beginners): A free, open-source 21-lesson course. Lessons are either "Learn" (concepts) or "Build" (code in Python and TypeScript where possible). Pick the lessons you need; they do not have to be taken in order.
- Prompt Engineering Guide by DAIR.AI (https://www.promptingguide.ai/): A free, community-maintained reference covering prompting techniques, with examples and links to the papers behind them. Use it as a lookup when you want to name and try a technique such as few-shot, chain-of-thought or ReAct.
- Anthropic prompt engineering documentation (https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/prompt-engineering/overview): Vendor docs, but the habits transfer to other models: be explicit, show examples, structure your inputs clearly, and iterate against a small set of test cases. Free to read; running the examples needs API access.
- OpenAI prompt engineering guide (https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/prompt-engineering): OpenAI's official guidance on writing prompts and structuring messages. Read it alongside another vendor's guide: where the two agree, you can trust the advice to travel across models. Free to read; API use is billed.
- Building Effective Agents: workflows vs agents (https://www.anthropic.com/research/building-effective-agents): A calm essay that separates predefined workflows from model-directed agents and lays out five composable patterns. Its main advice is to start with the simplest thing that works and add complexity only when it measurably helps.
- LLM Powered Autonomous Agents by Lilian Weng (https://lilianweng.github.io/posts/2023-06-23-agent/): A thorough overview of agents built around a language model, organised around planning, memory and tool use, with pointers to the research behind each. A good map of the territory before you pick a framework.
- LangGraph: stateful, long-running agent orchestration (https://github.com/langchain-ai/langgraph): MIT-licensed, low-level framework for agents modelled as stateful graphs, with durable execution so a run can resume after a failure. Reach for it when a plain loop stops being enough and you need control over state and flow.
- Model Context Protocol: the official introduction (https://modelcontextprotocol.io/): Home of the open protocol that lets AI applications connect to tools, data and prompts through a common interface. Start with the introduction and architecture pages, then build a small server of your own.
- MCP reference servers repository (https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/servers): Reference implementations of MCP servers, including a filesystem server. Read the source before writing your own; seeing how tools are declared and results returned is faster than reading the spec cold. Review any server before you run it.
- LlamaIndex documentation for building RAG over your data (https://developers.llamaindex.ai/python/framework/): Docs for an open-source framework that covers loading data, indexing, retrieval and query engines. A practical way to get a first retrieval pipeline running so you can see where quality really gets lost.
- Sentence Transformers: embeddings, retrieval and reranking (https://www.sbert.net/): The standard open-source Python library for computing text embeddings and running rerankers, with thousands of pretrained models on the Hugging Face Hub. Runs locally and for free; a good default for semantic search prototypes.
- Ollama: run open models locally with one command (https://github.com/ollama/ollama): Open-source runner that pulls a model and serves it with ollama run, plus a local REST API on port 11434. The quickest route to trying open models offline; customise behaviour later with a Modelfile.
- llama.cpp: C/C++ inference for local models (https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp): The engine behind much of the local-model ecosystem, running GGUF models on CPUs and GPUs. It includes llama-server with an OpenAI-compatible API. Choose it when you want control over quantisation, context size and offload.
- Open WebUI: a self-hosted chat interface for local models (https://github.com/open-webui/open-webui): Open-source, self-hosted web interface designed to run fully offline. It connects to Ollama or any OpenAI-compatible API, so you can give a team a familiar chat UI over models you host yourself.
- Anthropic's open skills repository (https://github.com/anthropics/skills): A repository of example Agent Skills: folders of instructions, scripts and resources that an agent loads when relevant. Study a few before writing your own; the structure and tone of the descriptions are the useful lesson.
- Agent Skills: the open format (https://agentskills.io): Documentation for the open Agent Skills format, built around a SKILL.md file with a name and description plus optional scripts and references. Read this to see what stays portable between tools that support skills.
- Aider: AI pair programming in your terminal (https://aider.chat/): Free, open-source terminal tool that edits code in your repository and works with git. It connects to most hosted models and to local ones, so you pay only your model provider, or nothing if you run locally.
- Continue: open-source coding agent for VS Code, JetBrains and the CLI (https://github.com/continuedev/continue): Apache-2.0 coding assistant available as a VS Code extension, JetBrains plugin and CLI. Pick it when you want an editor-integrated assistant that you can point at the model of your choice, hosted or local.
- MLflow for tracing and evaluating AI applications (https://mlflow.org/docs/latest/): Open-source platform that covers experiment tracking for classic models and tracing, evaluation and monitoring for LLM apps and agents. Choose it when you want one self-hostable tool across both kinds of work.
- Langfuse: open-source LLM observability (https://langfuse.com/docs): MIT-licensed, self-hostable platform for tracing LLM calls and agent runs. Use it to see what your application actually sent and received, which is the first step to debugging quality problems in production.
- OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications (https://genai.owasp.org/llm-top-10/): The community-maintained list of the main risks in LLM apps, led by prompt injection and including excessive agency, system prompt leakage and unbounded consumption. Use it as a review checklist before you ship.
- Simon Willison's prompt injection series (https://simonwillison.net/series/prompt-injection/): A running series of posts on prompt injection, the attack where untrusted text steers a model. Free and practical; read it to understand why filtering alone is not a defence and why architecture matters.
- The tool-use loop in four steps, and the stop reason that drives it (https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/overview): Tool use looks magical until you see the loop. You describe your tools (name, description, input schema), the model answers with a structured call instead of text, your code runs it, and you send the result back. The documented signal for "the model wants a tool" is stop_reason: "tool_use" plus tool_use blocks; your reply goes in a tool_result block carrying the matching tool_use_id.

Skeleton (Anthropic-style shapes, other providers differ in names but not in structure):
``python
messages = [{"role": "user", "content": question}]
for _ in range(8):  # hard cap on turns
    resp = client.messages.create(model=MODEL, max_tokens=1024,
                                  tools=tools, messages=messages)
    if resp.stop_reason != "tool_use":
        break
    messages.append({"role": "assistant", "content": resp.content})
    results = [run_tool(b) for b in resp.content if b.type == "tool_use"]
    messages.append({"role": "user", "content": results})
`
Two habits worth copying: always cap iterations, and have run_tool` return errors as text the model can read rather than raising.
- Write tool descriptions like an onboarding note for a new teammate (https://www.anthropic.com/research/writing-tools-for-agents): Agents fail on tools more often than on reasoning, and the fix is usually in the tool definition. The guidance in Anthropic's engineering write-up boils down to a few rules you can apply today:

- Name tools with a shared prefix per service or resource, so similar ones group together.
- Describe niche terms and query formats as you would to a new colleague, and prefer unambiguous parameters (user_id rather than user).
- Return high-signal fields (names, types) instead of raw UUIDs, and offer a concise/detailed switch.
- Paginate, filter and truncate by default so one call cannot flood the context.
- Make errors say how to fix the input.

A before/after:
``
before: search(q)  -> "Searches stuff"
after:  tickets_search(query, status="open", limit=10)
        "Full-text search over support tickets. status is one of
         open|closed|all. Returns title, id, assignee. Use
         tickets_get(id) for the full thread."
``
Then test with realistic multi-step tasks and read the transcripts to see where the agent hesitates.
- ReAct: let the model think between tool calls (https://arxiv.org/abs/2210.03629): The ReAct paper (Yao et al.) proposes interleaving reasoning traces with actions, so the model plans, acts, looks at what came back, and adjusts. Most agent loops you will meet today are descendants of that idea.

You can reproduce the pattern with plain prompting before reaching for a framework:
``
You can use these tools: search(query), read(url).
Work in this format until you can answer:
Thought: what you need to find out next
Action: one tool call
Observation: (filled in by the system)
...
Final: the answer, citing the observations you used
`
Your code does the boring part: parse the Action, run it, append the Observation, and call the model again. Stop on Final` or after a fixed number of rounds. Reading the paper is worthwhile for its failure analysis: the loop only helps when observations are reliable, so spend your effort on tool quality.
- Context engineering: compaction, notes and sub-agents (https://www.anthropic.com/research/effective-context-engineering-for-ai-agents): Long agent runs fail when the context fills with stale detail. Anthropic's engineering article frames context engineering as curating the smallest useful set of tokens at every model call, and names techniques for work that outgrows one window:

1. Compaction: summarise a nearly full conversation and continue in a fresh window.
2. Structured note-taking: the agent writes progress to a file and reloads it later.
3. Sub-agents: a worker explores in a clean context and hands back a condensed summary.
4. Just-in-time retrieval: keep paths and queries in context, load the content only when needed.

A cheap way to start is a notes file:
``
NOTES.md
## Goal
## Decisions made (and why)
## Done / Next
## Files that matter
``
Instruct the agent to update it after each milestone and to read it first in any new session. It costs a few lines and survives resets.
- Chain-of-thought prompting: show your reasoning steps in the examples (https://arxiv.org/abs/2201.11903): The chain-of-thought paper (Wei et al.) showed that including worked, step-by-step reasoning in few-shot examples lets large models solve multi-step problems they otherwise miss. The practical lesson: when accuracy matters, give the model room and a pattern for intermediate steps.

Template you can adapt:
``
Q: A pipeline has 3 stages taking 4, 7 and 5 minutes. Stages 2 and 3
   run in parallel after stage 1. How long end to end?
A: Stage 1 takes 4. Stages 2 and 3 run together, so they take
   max(7, 5) = 7. Total 4 + 7 = 11 minutes. Answer: 11

Q: <your real question>
A:
``
Two cautions. Check the final answer, not the story: fluent reasoning can still be wrong. And many current models reason by default, so test whether the explicit scaffold still improves results on your task before paying for the extra tokens.
- Lost in the Middle: where you put evidence in a long prompt matters (https://arxiv.org/abs/2307.03172): This paper measured how models use long contexts and found performance tends to be best when the relevant information sits at the beginning or end, and worse when it is buried in the middle. Models differ and have changed since, so treat it as a reason to test rather than a law.

A quick experiment for your own RAG or document-QA setup:
``
1. Take 20 questions with known answers.
2. For each, build the prompt with the answer-bearing passage at
   position first / middle / last among ~10 distractor passages.
3. Score accuracy per position.
``
If the middle is weaker, cheap mitigations include retrieving fewer, better passages, reranking so the strongest evidence lands near the edges, and repeating the question after the context. Whatever you change, rerun the same 20 questions so you know it helped.
- Typed outputs you can trust: validated results with Pydantic AI (https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic-ai): Free-form text is a poor interface between a model and your code. Pydantic AI, from the Pydantic team, lets you declare the shape you want and get back a validated object, which turns "parse and hope" into a typed contract.

Sketch (the model string is a placeholder, use whichever provider you have a key for):
``python
from pydantic import BaseModel
from pydantic_ai import Agent

class Ticket(BaseModel):
    severity: int
    summary: str

agent = Agent("provider:model-name", output_type=Ticket)
result = agent.run_sync("Checkout page 500s for all EU users")
print(result.output)   # a validated Ticket, not a string
``
Why it helps: invalid shapes are caught at the boundary, your IDE knows the fields, and tests can assert on real types. Keep the schema small and the field names self-explanatory, since the model reads them too.
- MCP in one picture: host, client, server and what each owns (https://modelcontextprotocol.io/docs/learn/architecture): MCP confuses people because three roles share one name. The architecture page separates them cleanly:

- Host: the AI application (an editor, a chat app, a CLI agent) that coordinates everything.
- Client: a component inside the host that keeps one connection to one server.
- Server: a program that provides context, locally over stdio or remotely over streamable HTTP.

Servers can expose three primitives: tools (functions the model can invoke), resources (data for context) and prompts (reusable templates). Clients discover tools with tools/list and invoke them with tools/call.

Mental model for debugging:
``
host -> creates one client per server
client -> server: tools/list   (what can you do?)
client -> server: tools/call   (do this, with these arguments)
``
When something misbehaves, ask which layer: is the server returning the wrong thing, is the client not surfacing it, or is the host not offering it to the model? The protocol evolves, so confirm details in the current spec.
- Anatomy of an MCP tool: schema, results and the isError flag (https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2026-07-28/server/tools): A tool in the MCP spec is a small contract: a unique name, a human-readable description, and an inputSchema written as JSON Schema. Servers can also declare an optional outputSchema for structured results.

``json
{
  "name": "tickets_search",
  "description": "Search support tickets by text. Returns id and title.",
  "inputSchema": {
    "type": "object",
    "properties": { "query": { "type": "string" } },
    "required": ["query"]
  }
}
`
The part people miss is error handling. Protocol errors (unknown tool, malformed request) are JSON-RPC errors. Failures inside the tool, such as a bad date format, should come back as a normal result with isError: true` and a message the model can act on, so it can correct itself and retry.

The spec also says there should be a human in the loop who can deny tool calls, and that clients should treat tool annotations as untrusted unless the server is trusted. Design your tools with both in mind.
- Before you install an MCP server: a security checklist from the spec authors (https://modelcontextprotocol.io/docs/2026-07-28/tutorials/security/security_best_practices): The MCP project publishes its own security best practices, and one section should change how you install things: local servers run with your privileges. A one-click config can launch an arbitrary command, so the page says clients must show the exact command and get explicit approval first.

A checklist you can apply as a user:
``
[ ] Read the exact command and arguments the config will run
[ ] Prefer servers whose source you have read or that you trust
[ ] Run local servers in a container or sandbox with minimal
    file and network access
[ ] Grant narrow scopes (read-only before write)
[ ] Prefer stdio for local servers; protect any local HTTP one
    with a token
``
If you build servers, the page also covers token passthrough (never accept tokens not issued for your server), SSRF when clients fetch URLs, hijacking of state handles, and scope minimisation. Skim those headings even if you only consume servers; they explain why the rules exist.
- Code execution with MCP: stop dragging every tool result through the model (https://www.anthropic.com/research/code-execution-with-mcp): Two costs appear when an agent talks to many MCP tools directly: every tool definition sits in context up front, and every intermediate result passes through the model. Anthropic's article describes an alternative: present MCP servers as code modules the agent can browse, and let it write code that calls them.

The shape of it:
``
servers/
  drive/getDocument.ts
  crm/updateRecord.ts

// agent-written code, run in a sandbox
const doc = await drive.getDocument({ id });
await crm.updateRecord({ id: leadId, notes: doc.content });
``
The document body never enters the model's context; only what the code chooses to return does. The article reports a large token reduction on its own example, but treat that number as illustrative. The trade-off is real: you now need a secure execution sandbox, resource limits and monitoring. Adopt it when tool counts or payload sizes hurt, not by default.
- Contextual retrieval: give every chunk a sentence of context before embedding (https://www.anthropic.com/research/contextual-retrieval): Chunking loses context: a chunk saying "revenue grew 3% over the previous quarter" no longer says which company or period. Contextual Retrieval fixes this by having a model write a short, chunk-specific note placing the chunk in its document, then prepending it before indexing.

A prompt in that spirit:
``
<document>{{WHOLE_DOCUMENT}}</document>
<chunk>{{CHUNK}}</chunk>
In one or two sentences, say where this chunk sits in the
document so it can be found by search. Answer with only that.
``
Index the augmented text for both embeddings and a BM25 keyword index, since exact identifiers are where embeddings slip. In Anthropic's own tests, this combination cut failed top-20 retrievals by 49 percent, and adding a reranker took it to 67 percent. Those are their datasets, so measure on yours. Cost note: it adds one model call per chunk at indexing time.
- Pick an embedding model with MTEB, then verify on your own queries (https://huggingface.co/spaces/mteb/leaderboard): The MTEB leaderboard on Hugging Face ranks embedding models across many tasks, which makes it a good place to build a shortlist. It is a bad place to make the final call, because your documents and queries are not the benchmark's.

A 30-minute procedure:
``
1. Filter the leaderboard by your language(s), a model size you
   can host, and a context length that fits your chunks.
2. Shortlist 3 models, including one small open model.
3. Write 30-50 real queries and note which document should win.
4. Embed your corpus with each model; compute recall@5.
5. Compare against cost, latency and storage dimensions.
``
Keep the same chunking across runs so you are testing the model, not the splitter. Also remember that switching models later means re-embedding everything, so record the model name and version next to the vectors.
- Vector search in Postgres: your first pgvector query and index (https://github.com/pgvector/pgvector): If you already run Postgres, pgvector lets you keep embeddings next to your relational data. The README's basics fit in a few lines:

``sql
CREATE EXTENSION vector;
CREATE TABLE items (id bigserial PRIMARY KEY, embedding vector(3));

-- nearest neighbours by L2 distance
SELECT * FROM items ORDER BY embedding <-> '[3,1,2]' LIMIT 5;

-- cosine distance, and an HNSW index that matches it
SELECT * FROM items ORDER BY embedding <=> '[3,1,2]' LIMIT 5;
CREATE INDEX ON items USING hnsw (embedding vector_cosine_ops);
`
Three details trip people up. The vector size (3 here) must equal your embedding model's output size. The operator in your query (<->, <=>) should match the operator class of the index, or the index will not be used. And <=> returns distance, so similarity is 1 - distance`. IVFFlat is the other index type if you need it.
- Evals begin with assertions: Hamel Husain's level-one tests (https://hamel.dev/blog/posts/evals/): Teams stall on evals because they imagine a platform. Hamel Husain's widely read post describes three levels, and the first is plain assertions, like you would write in pytest, that run fast and cheap while you develop. He also notes you keep adding tests as you see new failures in real data.

A starter in that spirit:
``python
import json, pytest
from myapp import answer

CASES = [
  ("What is your refund window?", "30 days"),
  ("Do you ship to Canada?", "Canada"),
]

@pytest.mark.parametrize("q,must_contain", CASES)
def test_mentions_fact(q, must_contain):
    assert must_contain in answer(q)

def test_valid_json():
    json.loads(answer("Return the order as JSON", fmt="json"))
``
Run it on every prompt change. Each production bug becomes a new case. Later levels (reading traces, model-graded checks, A/B tests) build on this habit,.
- A first prompt eval in a YAML file with promptfoo (https://www.promptfoo.dev/docs/intro/): Promptfoo is an open-source tool that treats prompts like testable code: you declare prompts, providers and test cases, run them, and compare. Its docs describe the cycle as defining test cases, running them, then iterating.

A minimal config shape (provider ids vary, check the docs for yours):
``yaml
# promptfooconfig.yaml
prompts:
  - "Summarise in one sentence: {{text}}"
providers:
  - openai:<model-name>   # swap for your provider id
tests:
  - vars: { text: "The deploy failed because the config key was missing." }
    assert:
      - type: icontains
        value: config
      - type: llm-rubric
        value: "Is a single sentence and does not invent causes"
`
Run npx promptfoo@latest eval and then npx promptfoo@latest view` to compare outputs side by side. Use cheap deterministic assertions first, and add the rubric-graded ones only for qualities you cannot check with a string match. Swapping providers lets you see the cost-quality trade-off on your own cases.
- LLM-as-judge works, and it has biases you must control for (https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.05685): The MT-Bench paper (Zheng et al.) studied using strong models to grade other models' answers. Its finding was encouraging: strong judges agreed with human preferences about as often as humans agree with each other. It also listed biases: position bias, verbosity bias and self-enhancement bias (favouring text from the same model family).

Controls you can add when you build a judge:
``
- Pairwise grading: run each comparison twice with A/B swapped;
  count only consistent verdicts.
- Rubrics: ask for a score on named criteria, not "which is better".
- Length: tell the judge not to reward length; check for correlation.
- Self-preference: avoid grading a model with itself.
- Calibration: have a human label 30 examples and compare.
``
Treat the judge as an instrument that needs calibration against human labels on your task, not as ground truth.
- Inspect AI: write an eval as a task, a solver and a scorer (https://inspect.aisi.org.uk/): Inspect is an open-source framework for LLM evaluations from the UK AI Security Institute. Its structure is worth learning even if you end up using something else: an eval is a Task with a dataset, a solver (how the model is driven) and a scorer (how answers are graded).

The docs' own example has this shape:
``python
from inspect_ai import Task, task
from inspect_ai.scorer import model_graded_qa
from inspect_ai.solver import generate

@task
def my_eval():
    return Task(
        dataset=my_dataset,          # your samples
        solver=generate(),
        scorer=model_graded_qa(),
    )
`
Run it with inspect eval my_eval.py --model provider/model`. The decorator registers the function so the CLI can find it by name. The project also ships a large collection of pre-built evaluations, which is a good place to see how experienced teams structure datasets and scorers.
- Shape a local model with an Ollama Modelfile (https://docs.ollama.com/modelfile): Once Ollama is installed, a Modelfile lets you save a configured variant instead of retyping settings. It starts from a base with FROM (a model name or a local GGUF file) and can set parameters and a system prompt.

``
# Modelfile
FROM llama3.2
PARAMETER temperature 0.2
SYSTEM """
You are a terse code reviewer. Point out bugs first, style last.
"""
`
Build and run it:
`
ollama create reviewer -f Modelfile
ollama run reviewer
``
Why bother: the behaviour travels with the name, so teammates get the same setup, and you can keep several variants (a strict reviewer, a loose brainstormer) side by side. Keep the SYSTEM text short and testable. Check the Modelfile reference for the full list of instructions and parameters, since they change between releases.
- Serve a local model over an OpenAI-style API with llama-server (https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/blob/master/tools/server/README.md): llama.cpp ships llama-server, an HTTP server that exposes OpenAI-compatible endpoints such as /v1/chat/completions. Because many tools can target an OpenAI-style base URL, this lets editors, scripts and agents use a model on your machine.

``
llama-server -m ./model.gguf -c 8192 --port 8080 -ngl auto

curl localhost:8080/v1/chat/completions \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"messages":[{"role":"user","content":"Say hi in five words"}]}'
`
What the flags do: -m picks the GGUF file, -c sets the context window, --port chooses the port (set it explicitly rather than relying on defaults), and -ngl controls how many layers go to the GPU. If you bind beyond localhost with --host, add --api-key`, since the server has no authentication by default. Larger context uses more memory, so raise it only as far as you need.
- Run vLLM when one local user becomes many (https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/): Ollama and llama.cpp shine for one person on one machine. When several users or jobs hit the same model, throughput starts to matter, and vLLM is built for that. Its README highlights PagedAttention for managing attention memory, continuous batching of incoming requests, and an OpenAI-compatible API server.

Starting point on a GPU machine:
``
pip install vllm
vllm serve <model-id-from-hugging-face>
# then point any OpenAI-style client at the server's /v1 URL
``
Decide before you deploy:
- Will the model fit in GPU memory with room for the KV cache?
- What concurrency and context length do you really need?
- Who can reach the endpoint, and is there an API key in front?
- How will you monitor latency and queueing?
Load-test with your real prompt lengths rather than a toy example; batching behaviour depends heavily on them.
- Docker Model Runner: pull and run a model like an image (https://docs.docker.com/ai/model-runner/): If your team already lives in Docker, Docker Model Runner offers a familiar workflow for local models. The docs show commands in the style of the image CLI:

``
docker model pull ai/smollm2
docker model run ai/smollm2
`
You can also configure settings such as context size with docker model configure`, per the docs. The appeal is consistency: models are pulled by name from a registry, versions are explicit, and the same muscle memory covers containers and models. It is a reasonable choice for developer machines and CI experiments where you want repeatable pulls without installing yet another runner.

Practical tips: pin a specific tag in scripts rather than relying on a default, keep an eye on disk use since models are large, and confirm what hardware acceleration your platform supports in the current docs, because that varies by OS.
- QLoRA: fine-tune a large model on modest hardware (https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.14314): QLoRA (Dettmers et al.) backpropagates through a frozen, 4-bit quantised base model into small LoRA adapters. The authors report fine-tuning a 65B-parameter model on a single 48GB GPU while keeping full 16-bit fine-tuning quality, which is why the technique spread so widely.

You do not need to implement it. The Hugging Face PEFT library packages LoRA-style methods, and the shape of the setup is:
``python
from peft import LoraConfig, get_peft_model

config = LoraConfig(r=16, lora_alpha=32, task_type="CAUSAL_LM")
model = get_peft_model(base_model, config)
model.print_trainable_parameters()
``
Before reaching for fine-tuning, check three cheaper options: better prompts, retrieval, and a small eval set that shows what is actually failing. Fine-tuning is best for style, format and narrow behaviours, not for loading in fast-changing facts. Keep the data clean; adapters faithfully learn your mistakes too.
- Write your first SKILL.md: a description that triggers, a body that guides (https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/agent-skills/overview): A skill is a folder with a SKILL.md file. Its frontmatter needs a name (lowercase letters, numbers, hyphens; up to 64 characters) and a description (non-empty, up to 1,024 characters). The description is what the agent matches your request against, so it must say what the skill does and when to use it.

``markdown
---
name: release-notes
description: Drafts release notes from merged pull requests. Use when
  the user asks for a changelog, release notes or "what shipped".
---
# Release notes
1. List merged PRs since the last tag (git log --merges).
2. Group by: Features, Fixes, Internal.
3. One line each, user-facing language, link the PR.
See TEMPLATE.md for the output format.
``
The docs describe loading in stages: only name and description are always in context, the body loads when triggered, and extra files or scripts load only when referenced. So keep the body focused and push detail into side files. Only install skills from sources you trust, since they can include scripts.
- Skill hygiene from the open spec: size, structure, validation (https://agentskills.io/specification): The Agent Skills specification is the portable part: a directory with SKILL.md, plus optional scripts/, references/ and assets/. Notably, the name must match the parent directory name, must not start or end with a hyphen, and must not contain consecutive hyphens.

Guidance from the spec worth adopting:
``
- Keep SKILL.md under about 500 lines; recommended < 5000 tokens.
- Move reference material to separate files, one level deep.
- Keep each reference file focused; they load on demand.
- Write a description with concrete trigger words, not "helps
  with PDFs".
- Validate: skills-ref validate ./my-skill
`
Optional fields include license, compatibility (for environment needs such as required tools), metadata and an experimental allowed-tools`. Tool support for the optional fields varies, so test in the agent you actually use. A good habit is to write the description last, once you know what the skill really covers.
- Give your coding agent a way to check its own work (https://code.claude.com/docs/en/best-practices): The Claude Code best-practices page makes a point that applies to any coding agent: give it a check to run. If the agent can run tests, a linter or a build and read the result, it can correct itself instead of handing you plausible-looking code. (The tool itself needs a paid plan or API access; the habits are free and transfer.)

Practical steps:
``
1. Put the one command that proves "done" in your instructions
   file, e.g.  npm test && npm run lint
2. Ask for a specific outcome, not "improve this":
   "Fix the failing test in billing.spec.ts without changing
    its assertions."
3. Keep the instructions file short; every line costs attention
   on every task.
4. If a rule must never be broken, don't rely on prose;
   enforce it with a hook or permission rule.
``
The docs make that last distinction explicit: instructions are guidance the model can weigh, while hooks and permissions are deterministic. Choose accordingly.
- AGENTS.md: one instructions file for many coding agents (https://agents.md): AGENTS.md is a plain Markdown file at the repository root, described by its site as a README for agents. The same page lists many supporting tools, including Codex, Cursor, Aider, Gemini CLI, Zed, Windsurf and GitHub Copilot's coding agent, so one file can serve several of them. Nested files in subdirectories can tailor guidance for sub-projects.

Recommended contents from the site are project overview, build and test commands, code style, testing expectations, security notes and commit or PR rules. A compact version:
``markdown
# AGENTS.md
## Setup
- Install: pnpm install
- Test: pnpm test (must pass before any commit)
## Conventions
- TypeScript strict; no default exports
- Small PRs; conventional commit messages
## Do not
- Edit files under /generated
``
Keep it factual and short, and update it when commands change. A stale instruction file is worse than none, because the agent will follow it confidently.
- Copilot custom instructions: repository-wide and path-specific (https://docs.github.com/en/copilot/how-tos/configure-custom-instructions/add-repository-instructions): GitHub's docs describe two levels of repository instructions for Copilot. Repository-wide guidance lives in .github/copilot-instructions.md. Path-specific guidance goes in files named NAME.instructions.md under .github/instructions, each with frontmatter whose applyTo takes glob patterns.

``markdown
---
applyTo: "/*.ts,/*.tsx"
---
Use named exports. Prefer zod for runtime validation.
Tests live next to the file as *.test.ts.
``
The docs also say AGENTS.md is supported, with the nearest file in the tree taking precedence, and that a single CLAUDE.md or GEMINI.md at the root can be used instead. So if your team mixes assistants, you can often share one set of rules rather than maintain three. Scope rules by path to keep each instruction short and relevant, and review what the assistant actually does with them in a real pull request.
- The lethal trifecta: the three capabilities you must not combine carelessly (https://simonwillison.net/2025/Jun/16/the-lethal-trifecta/): Simon Willison names three capabilities that become dangerous together in an agent: access to your private data, exposure to untrusted content, and the ability to communicate externally in a way that could exfiltrate data. If one agent has all three, an attacker who can get text in front of it may be able to steer it into sending your data out.

Use it as a design review:
``
For each agent or tool bundle, answer:
1. Private data?     (mail, repos, tickets, secrets)
2. Untrusted input?  (web pages, inbound email, issues, PDFs)
3. Outbound channel? (HTTP requests, email, links that load images)
If all three are yes, remove one of them.
``
Removing the outbound channel (no arbitrary network, no auto-loading links) is often the cheapest cut. He also points out that mixing tools from different MCP servers can assemble the trifecta without anyone intending to. Guardrail prompts help but are not a reliable boundary; architecture is.
- Indirect prompt injection: the attack arrives inside the data (https://arxiv.org/abs/2302.12173): Greshake et al. studied indirect prompt injection: instead of typing malicious instructions to a model, an attacker plants them in content the application will later retrieve, such as a web page or document. The model reads them as part of its context and may follow them. Retrieval and tool use are what make this practical.

Defensive habits to apply when you build:
``
- Treat everything retrieved as data, never as instructions;
  mark it clearly as untrusted in the prompt.
- Give the model the minimum tools and scopes for the task.
- Require human confirmation for side effects (send, delete, pay).
- Strip or block outbound channels that data could leave through.
- Log tool calls so you can audit what the model was steered into.
- Red-team with your own planted instructions in test documents.
``
Labelling data as untrusted lowers risk but does not remove it, so the structural controls matter most. Read the paper's threat taxonomy to see how many routes into a context window exist.

### Core developer skills
The skills every developer leans on, whatever the stack: version control, the terminal, containers, databases, testing, security and the career side of the job.
- Git Mistake First Aid: Plain-English Recovery Recipes (https://dangitgit.com/): A short, no-jargon page of recipes for the Git situations that make people panic: committed to the wrong branch, a bad commit message, an undo that went too far. Bookmark it, then read the explanations so the fix stops feeling like magic.
- Atlassian Git Tutorials: Workflows, Merging and Rewriting History (https://www.atlassian.com/git/tutorials): Free, well-illustrated tutorials that go beyond commit and push: branching workflows, merge versus rebase, undoing changes and rewriting history. A good second Git resource once the basics are comfortable and you start working in a team.
- Linux Journey: A Gentle Path From First Command to Confident User (https://linuxjourney.com/): Free lessons in small chunks covering the command line, users and permissions, processes, networking and more. Start here if the terminal still feels foreign, and use the quizzes to check what actually stuck before moving on.
- explainshell: Paste a Command, See What Every Part Means (https://explainshell.com/): Paste any shell command and each flag and argument is matched to the relevant excerpt from its manual page. Handy for decoding a copied one-liner before you run it, and for learning how pipes and options fit together.
- BashPitfalls: The Shell Mistakes Everyone Makes Once (https://mywiki.wooledge.org/BashPitfalls): A catalogue of common Bash bugs, each with a short explanation and a safer pattern: unquoted variables, parsing ls output, misuse of test. Read it before writing scripts that will run unattended, then run ShellCheck on what you have.
- Brendan Gregg on Linux Performance: Tools Mapped to the Stack (https://www.brendangregg.com/linuxperf.html): A reference page that maps observability and tracing tools to the parts of a Linux system they inspect, with diagrams and talks. Reach for it when a box is slow and you need to know which tool answers which question.
- The USE Method: A Checklist for Finding Bottlenecks (https://www.brendangregg.com/usemethod.html): A simple method for performance problems: for every resource, check utilization, saturation and errors. It gives you a systematic order of questions instead of guessing, and applies to CPUs, disks, networks and queues alike.
- Docker Build Best Practices: Smaller, Faster, Safer Images (https://docs.docker.com/build/building/best-practices/): The official guidance on writing Dockerfiles: choosing base images, multi-stage builds, layer caching, pinning and cleanup. Use it as a review checklist the next time an image feels bloated or a build keeps missing the cache.
- iximiuz Labs: Hands-On Container and Linux Playgrounds (https://labs.iximiuz.com/): Browser-based playgrounds and challenges for containers, Linux internals and Kubernetes, with a number of free ones. Good for building a real mental model of what a container is, by poking at namespaces and cgroups yourself.
- Use The Index, Luke: A Free Book on SQL Indexing (https://use-the-index-luke.com/): A free online guide to how database indexes work and how to design them for real queries. It covers the anatomy of an index, the WHERE clause, sorting and joins. Read it when queries are slow and you want to understand why.
- PostgreSQL Exercises: Practice SQL Against a Real Database (https://pgexercises.com/): Graded SQL exercises on a small club-membership schema, running in the browser with hints and worked answers. Moves from simple selects to joins, aggregates and window functions, so it is a good place to practice after a first course.
- Learn OpenAPI: The Official Introduction to Describing APIs (https://learn.openapis.org/): The official learning site from the OpenAPI Initiative explains how to describe an HTTP API in a machine-readable contract. Start here before generating docs, mocks or client code, so the spec becomes the shared source of truth for the team.
- Microsoft Web API Design Best Practices: A Practical Checklist (https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/architecture/best-practices/api-design): A thorough guide to designing HTTP APIs: resource naming, methods and status codes, pagination, versioning and async operations. Useful as a review checklist for a new API, whatever stack or cloud you build on.
- System Design Primer: A Map of Scaling Concepts and Trade-offs (https://github.com/donnemartin/system-design-primer): A large open-source study guide covering load balancers, caching, databases, queues and consistency, with diagrams and example designs. Use it to build vocabulary and a mental catalogue of trade-offs before design discussions or interviews.
- Amazon Builders Library: How Large Systems Fail and Recover (https://aws.amazon.com/builders-library/): Articles by Amazon engineers on operating distributed systems, including timeouts, retries with backoff and jitter, and avoiding overload. Read them when you design for failure and want the reasoning behind patterns, not only the names.
- The Practical Test Pyramid: Deciding What to Test Where (https://martinfowler.com/articles/practical-test-pyramid.html): A long, example-driven article on balancing unit, integration, contract and end-to-end tests. Read it when your suite is slow or flaky, or when you cannot decide at which level a new test belongs.
- Software Engineering at Google: The Testing Overview Chapter (https://abseil.io/resources/swe-book/html/ch11.html): A free chapter on why tests matter at scale, how test size relates to speed and reliability, and what makes tests maintainable. A good grounding for arguing about test strategy with evidence rather than taste.
- OWASP Top 10: The Standard Awareness List for Web Risks (https://owasp.org/www-project-top-ten/): The widely referenced list of the most critical web application security risks, with explanations and prevention advice for each. Use it as a shared vocabulary for reviews and threat conversations, and as a map of what to study next.
- Hacksplaining: Interactive Lessons on How Attacks Work (https://www.hacksplaining.com/lessons): Short, free, interactive lessons that walk through attacks such as SQL injection and cross-site scripting, then show how to prevent them in code. A friendly way to see the attacker view before you dig into deeper labs.
- AWS Well-Architected Framework: A Review Lens for Cloud Designs (https://aws.amazon.com/architecture/well-architected/): A set of questions and best practices across areas like security, reliability, cost and operations. Even outside AWS it is a handy checklist for design reviews, and the questions are free to read without an account.
- Microsoft Learn: Free Cloud Fundamentals and Role-Based Paths (https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/training/): Free, structured modules and learning paths on cloud concepts, networking, identity and DevOps, many with sandbox environments. A solid starting point if you want guided practice instead of piecing docs together alone.
- Tech Interview Handbook: Resume, Coding and Behavioral Prep (https://www.techinterviewhandbook.org/): A free, curated handbook on the whole job search: resumes, preparing for coding rounds, behavioral questions and negotiation. Use it as a single organized starting point, then dive into the sections that match your stage.
- StaffEng Guides: Growing Beyond Senior Engineer (https://staffeng.com/guides/): Practical guides on technical leadership at senior levels: scope, influence, working with leadership and writing for decisions. Helpful even earlier, since it shows which habits you can start building now.
- NeetCode Roadmap: A Structured Path Through Coding Problems (https://neetcode.io/roadmap): A free roadmap that groups algorithm problems by pattern, such as two pointers, graphs and dynamic programming, with a visual map of dependencies. Handy for turning random practice into a deliberate plan for coding interviews.
- Google Technical Writing Courses: Clearer Docs, Issues and Emails (https://developers.google.com/tech-writing): Free, short courses on writing clear technical prose: precise words, active voice, organizing documents and reviewing drafts. Useful for design docs, pull request descriptions and any message that others must act on.
- Undo the Undo: Recovering Lost Commits With git reflog (https://git-scm.com/docs/git-reflog): Git rarely deletes work right away. Every time HEAD or a branch tip moves, the reflog records where it was, so a botched reset or rebase is usually recoverable.

``bash
git reflog                  # find the entry from before the mistake
git branch rescue HEAD@{3}  # pin that state to a new branch
git switch rescue
`

Read entries like HEAD@{3} as "where HEAD was three moves ago". Create a branch from the right one before doing anything else, because a branch name is what keeps commits safe from cleanup.

Two limits worth knowing: the reflog is local to your clone, and entries expire. By default unreachable ones are pruned after about 30 days and reachable ones after about 90, controlled by gc.reflogExpire and gc.reflogExpireUnreachable`. So recover soon, and never rely on it as a backup.
- Challenge: Rescue a Branch You Just Deleted (https://git-scm.com/docs/git-branch): Ten minutes, a scratch repo, no risk. Prove to yourself that a deleted branch is not gone.

``bash
git init rescue-lab && cd rescue-lab
git commit --allow-empty -m "base"
git switch -c feature/payments
echo "important work" > pay.txt && git add pay.txt && git commit -m "add payments"
git switch -            # back to the first branch
git branch -D feature/payments
`

Now recover it:

1. Run git reflog and find the "add payments" commit.
2. Run git branch feature/payments <sha> with that hash.
3. Check with git log feature/payments --oneline and confirm pay.txt exists after switching.

Stretch goal: repeat the exercise, but this time lose the commit by running git reset --hard HEAD~1 on the branch itself, and recover it the same way. Notice that the capital D in -D` only means "delete even if unmerged"; the commits stay in the object store until garbage collection removes them.
- Interactive Rebase: Tidy a Branch Before Asking for Review (https://git-scm.com/docs/git-rebase): A reviewer reads your history as a story, so make it readable. Interactive rebase lets you reshape local commits before they are shared.

``bash
git rebase -i origin/main
`

In the editor, change the word at the start of a line:
- reword to fix a message
- squash or fixup to fold a commit into the one above it
- drop to remove it, and reorder lines to reorder commits

A neat habit: when you spot a fix for an earlier commit, record it with git commit --fixup <sha>, then later run git rebase -i --autosquash origin/main and Git arranges the fixup commits for you.

Rewriting changes commit hashes, so only do it on commits nobody else has based work on. If you must update a branch you already pushed, prefer git push --force-with-lease over --force, because it refuses to overwrite commits you have not seen. If the rebase goes wrong, git rebase --abort` restores where you started.
- Find the Commit That Broke It: Automated git bisect (https://git-scm.com/docs/git-bisect): When a regression appeared "sometime in the last 200 commits", binary search beats reading diffs. Git bisect halves the range each step, so even a few hundred commits take around eight checks.

``bash
git bisect start
git bisect bad                 # current commit is broken
git bisect good v2.3.0         # a commit or tag known to be fine
git bisect run ./check.sh
git bisect reset
`

The script passed to run decides the verdict by exit code: 0 means good, 1 to 127 (except 125) means bad, and 125 means "cannot test this commit, skip it". A script can be as small as a single test command, for example npm test -- -t "login" or a curl that fails on a bad status.

Tips: keep the script outside the repository tree or untracked so checkouts do not remove it, and make sure the build step is inside the script. Finish with git bisect reset` to return to your branch.
- Scrub a Leaked File From History With git filter-repo (https://github.com/newren/git-filter-repo): If a credentials file or a huge binary landed in history, deleting it in a new commit does not remove it from old ones. The maintained tool for rewriting history is git filter-repo, which the Git project itself points to in place of filter-branch.

``bash
git clone --no-local your-repo scrub && cd scrub
git filter-repo --invert-paths --path config/secrets.env
git remote add origin <url>
git push --force --all
``

Notes:
- It insists on a fresh clone as a safety check, so work on a copy.
- Every commit after the file's first appearance gets a new hash, so every collaborator must re-clone or carefully reset, and open pull requests will need attention.
- Forks, caches and CI logs may still hold the old data, and hosting platforms can keep unreachable commits for a while.

The key point for secrets: assume they are compromised the moment they are pushed. Rotate the credential first; the history rewrite is cleanup, not remediation.
- Challenge: Find What Is Filling the Disk in Five Minutes (https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man1/du.1.html): A full disk takes services down quietly, so practice the hunt before you need it.

1. Check which filesystem is full: df -h
2. Check inodes too, since many tiny files can exhaust them with space to spare: df -i
3. Descend one level at a time:

``bash
sudo du -xh --max-depth=1 /var 2>/dev/null | sort -h | tail -n 10
`

Repeat on the largest directory until you reach the culprit. The -x flag keeps du on one filesystem, and sort -h understands sizes like 4.0K and 2.1G.

Your task: run this on your own machine or a VM, write down the three biggest directories under /var, and explain what each one is for. Bonus: a deleted file that a process still holds open keeps using space. Look for it with sudo lsof +L1`, which lists open files whose link count is zero.
- Inspect a Running Process Through /proc (https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man5/proc.5.html): Linux exposes live process state as files, so you can answer many "what is this thing doing?" questions with cat and ls, even on a minimal container image without extra tools.

``bash
PID=$(pgrep -n myapp)
tr '\0' ' ' < /proc/$PID/cmdline; echo   # exact command line
grep -E 'State|VmRSS|Threads' /proc/$PID/status
ls -l /proc/$PID/fd | head                # open files and sockets
cat /proc/$PID/limits                     # per-process limits
ls -l /proc/$PID/cwd /proc/$PID/exe       # where it runs and what it is
`

The command line is NUL-separated, hence the tr. A growing count in fd points to a descriptor leak, and Max open files in limits tells you how close you are to the ceiling. VmRSS is resident memory.

You can read your own processes freely; other users' details need root. The manual page above documents every file, and is worth skimming once for maps, smaps and environ`.
- Make Bash Scripts Fail Loudly: set -euo pipefail Explained (https://www.gnu.org/software/bash/manual/html_node/The-Set-Builtin.html): A script that keeps going after an error can do real damage. A common opening is:

``bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail
trap 'echo "failed at line $LINENO" >&2' ERR
`

- -e exits when a command fails
- -u treats an unset variable as an error, catching typos like $DIR_NAEM
- -o pipefail makes a pipeline fail if any stage fails, not just the last

Know the limits. -e is ignored in places such as an if condition or the left side of && and ||, and in a few subshell cases, so it is a safety net, not a substitute for checking results you care about. Tolerate an expected failure explicitly: grep -q foo file || true.

Also quote your variables, and run ShellCheck. The manual page linked here lists every option precisely, including the exceptions to -e`.
- Trace a Hung Process With strace (https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man1/strace.1.html): When a process is stuck and the logs are silent, strace shows what it asks the kernel to do. A blocked read on a socket, a connect to the wrong address, or endless open failures all stand out.

``bash
sudo strace -f -tt -T -s 200 -o trace.txt -p <PID>
strace -f -e trace=network -o net.txt ./myprogram
strace -c ./myprogram        # syscall count and time summary
`

Meaning of the flags: -f follows child threads and processes, -tt adds timestamps, -T shows time spent inside each call, -s lengthens printed strings, and -o writes to a file. Filtering with -e trace=` cuts the noise.

Read the last lines first: if the final line is a call that has not returned, that is where it is stuck. Expect a slowdown while tracing, and attaching may need root or relaxed ptrace settings. Avoid tracing a busy production process for long.
- Multi-Stage Docker Builds: Ship the Binary, Not the Toolchain (https://docs.docker.com/build/building/multi-stage/): Build tools, caches and source code have no business in your runtime image. A multi-stage build compiles in one stage and copies only the result into a small final one.

``dockerfile
FROM golang:1 AS build
WORKDIR /src
COPY go.mod go.sum ./
RUN go mod download
COPY . .
RUN CGO_ENABLED=0 go build -o /out/app .

FROM scratch
COPY --from=build /out/app /app
USER 10001:10001
ENTRYPOINT ["/app"]
`

Results: a much smaller image, a smaller attack surface, and faster pulls. Copying the dependency files before the source keeps the download layer cached until they change.

Caveats: scratch has no shell, CA certificates or timezone data, so copy those in or choose a minimal base such as a distroless one if you need them. Interpreted languages follow the same idea: install dependencies in a builder stage and copy the prepared directory over. You can also stop at a stage with docker build --target build .` to debug it.
- Challenge: Lock Down a Container and Prove It Worked (https://docs.docker.com/reference/cli/docker/container/run/): Run a container with fewer privileges, then verify each restriction yourself. Needs Docker and about fifteen minutes.

``bash
docker run --rm -it \
  --user 10001:10001 \
  --read-only --tmpfs /tmp \
  --cap-drop=ALL \
  --security-opt no-new-privileges \
  --pids-limit 100 --memory 256m \
  alpine sh
`

Inside the container, test:
1. id should show uid 10001, not root.
2. touch /x should fail with a read-only filesystem error, while touch /tmp/x succeeds.
3. grep CapEff /proc/self/status should show all zeros, meaning no effective capabilities.

Now loosen one flag at a time and notice what changes. Then ask the harder question for your own service: which flags does it actually need, and what breaks when you remove the rest? Put the result into a Compose file or Kubernetes security context so it is repeatable. Never use --privileged` as a shortcut to make an error disappear.
- Read a Postgres Query Plan Without Guessing (https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/using-explain.html): The plan tells you what the database did, so you can stop guessing at indexes.

``sql
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)
SELECT * FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 42 ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 10;
`

What to look for:
- The scan type: Seq Scan reads the whole table, Index Scan and Bitmap Heap Scan use an index.
- Estimated versus actual rows. A big gap means stale statistics (run ANALYZE) or a misleading predicate.
- Rows Removed by Filter: many rows read and thrown away suggests a missing or wrong index.
- Timing is per node and may be multiplied by the loop count.

Important: ANALYZE really executes the statement. For writes, wrap it: BEGIN; EXPLAIN ANALYZE UPDATE ...; ROLLBACK;`. And a sequential scan on a small table is often the right choice, so judge by timing, not by the node name alone.
- Challenge: Fix a Slow Query With the Right Composite Index (https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/indexes-multicolumn.html): Build a million-row table, watch a query struggle, then fix it. About twenty minutes in PostgreSQL.

``sql
CREATE TABLE orders AS
SELECT g AS id,
       (random()*10000)::int AS customer_id,
       now() - random() * interval '365 days' AS created_at
FROM generate_series(1, 1000000) g;
ANALYZE orders;

EXPLAIN ANALYZE
SELECT * FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 42 ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 10;

CREATE INDEX orders_cust_created ON orders (customer_id, created_at);
ANALYZE orders;
-- rerun the EXPLAIN ANALYZE above
`

Compare the plans and timings. The index lets the database jump to one customer and read rows already in date order, so no sorting is needed.

Then experiment: drop it and create (created_at, customer_id)` instead. Why is the first query worse now? Multicolumn B-tree indexes are most useful when the query constrains the leading columns, so put equality columns first, then the sort or range column.
- Isolation Levels in Plain Terms: Pick One on Purpose (https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/transaction-iso.html): Transactions are not automatically safe from each other. In PostgreSQL the default is Read Committed: each statement sees data committed before it started, so two reads in one transaction can differ.

A classic bug is read-modify-write:

``sql
-- risky: two sessions can both read 100 and write 90
SELECT balance FROM accounts WHERE id = 1;
UPDATE accounts SET balance = 90 WHERE id = 1;

-- safe: let the database do it atomically
UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - 10
WHERE id = 1 AND balance >= 10;
`

Your options, roughly from lightest to strongest: an atomic UPDATE like the one above, SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` to lock the row, or a stricter level such as Repeatable Read or Serializable.

The catch with the strict levels: the database may abort a transaction with a serialization failure (SQLSTATE 40001), and your code must retry the whole transaction. In PostgreSQL, Read Uncommitted behaves like Read Committed. Other databases differ, so check yours.
- Idempotency Keys: Make Retried POST Requests Safe (https://docs.stripe.com/api/idempotent_requests): Networks drop responses, not just requests. If a client retries a payment after a timeout, you must not charge twice. The standard fix is a client-generated idempotency key.

Stripe documents a good reference design: the client sends an Idempotency-Key header with a random value such as a UUID (their keys can be up to 255 characters), and the server stores the first result and replays it for retries. Reusing a key with different parameters is rejected.

A minimal server-side shape:

``sql
CREATE TABLE idempotency (
  key text PRIMARY KEY,
  request_hash text NOT NULL,
  response jsonb,
  created_at timestamptz DEFAULT now()
);
``

1. Insert the key before doing work. A unique violation means it is a retry or a concurrent duplicate.
2. If the stored hash differs from this request, return an error.
3. Run the operation and save the response in the same transaction where possible.
4. Expire old keys; Stripe prunes after at least 24 hours.

GET and DELETE are already idempotent by definition, so keys matter mainly for POST.
- Challenge: Replace Offset Pagination With a Keyset Cursor (https://use-the-index-luke.com/no-offset): OFFSET pagination gets slower the deeper you go, and it can skip or repeat rows when data changes between pages. Keyset pagination fixes both. Try it in thirty minutes on any SQL database with a table of a few hundred thousand rows.

Page one:

``sql
SELECT id, created_at FROM events
ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC
LIMIT 20;
`

Next page, using the last row you returned:

`sql
SELECT id, created_at FROM events
WHERE (created_at, id) < ($1, $2)
ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC
LIMIT 20;
`

Steps:
1. Create an index on (created_at, id).
2. Compare EXPLAIN output for this query against OFFSET 100000.
3. Encode (created_at, id) as an opaque base64 string and return it as next_cursor in your API response.

The tie-breaker id` matters because timestamps repeat. The trade-off: you lose jump-to-page-N, which is usually fine for feeds and exports.
- Change an API Without Breaking Anyone: Compatibility Rules (https://google.aip.dev/180): Clients you do not control will depend on every detail you expose. Google's API improvement proposal on backwards compatibility spells out what is safe within one major version.

Generally safe: adding new methods, new response fields, and optional request fields whose default preserves old behavior. Adding enum values to responses is allowed but risky, since clients may not handle unknown values, so document it.

Breaking: removing anything, renaming (which is removal plus addition), changing a field's type, changing a default, changing a value's format, or tightening semantics that clients rely on.

Habits that follow:
