- Make new request fields optional.
- Tell clients to ignore unknown response fields and handle unknown enum values.
- To rename, add the new name, keep the old one, deprecate it publicly, and remove it only in a new major version.
- Review diffs of your OpenAPI file in CI to catch accidental breaks.

When a break is truly necessary, version it and give people time to migrate.
- Cache-Aside Done Right: TTLs, Invalidation and Stampedes (https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/architecture/patterns/cache-aside): Cache-aside is the usual pattern: the application checks the cache, falls back to the database on a miss, and fills the cache itself.

``python
def get_user(uid):
    v = cache.get(f"user:{uid}")
    if v is not None:
        return v
    v = db.fetch_user(uid)
    cache.set(f"user:{uid}", v, ttl=300 + random.randint(0, 60))
    return v

def update_user(uid, data):
    db.update_user(uid, data)
    cache.delete(f"user:{uid}")   # delete, don't rewrite
``

Points to get right:
- Always set a TTL, so mistakes eventually heal. Add jitter so many keys do not expire together.
- On writes, update the database first and then delete the key. Deleting is simpler than rewriting.
- A hot key expiring can send many requests to the database at once. Let one request rebuild it while the others wait or serve slightly stale data.
- Decide whether caching "not found" is worth it, with a short TTL.

Remember the cache is an optimization; the system must still work, slowly, without it.
- At-Least-Once Queues Need Idempotent Consumers (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSSimpleQueueService/latest/SQSDeveloperGuide/sqs-visibility-timeout.html): Most queues promise at-least-once delivery. A message can arrive twice, so a consumer that is not safe to repeat will eventually bill someone twice.

Take SQS as a concrete example. A received message becomes invisible for the visibility timeout (default 30 seconds). If you do not delete it in time, it reappears and another consumer may process it. You can extend it with ChangeMessageVisibility, up to a 12-hour total limit.

Safe consumer recipe:
1. Pick a stable id: the message id or, better, a business id such as an order number.
2. In one database transaction, insert that id into a processed table with a unique constraint and apply the effect.
3. If the insert conflicts, skip the work.
4. Delete the message only after the transaction commits.
5. Set the timeout above your typical processing time, and configure a dead-letter queue so poison messages stop looping.

Alert on dead-letter queue depth and on message age, since those show trouble before users do.
- Challenge: Test Your Code With Properties, Not Just Examples (https://hypothesis.readthedocs.io/en/latest/quickstart.html): Example-based tests check what you thought of. Property-based tests check rules and let the library hunt for counterexamples. Try it in twenty minutes with Python.

``bash
pip install hypothesis pytest
`

`python
from hypothesis import given, strategies as st

@given(st.lists(st.integers()))
def test_sort_is_idempotent(xs):
    assert sorted(sorted(xs)) == sorted(xs)

@given(st.lists(st.integers()))
def test_sort_keeps_length(xs):
    assert len(sorted(xs)) == len(xs)
`

Run pytest. Now pick a function of your own and write a round-trip property, such as decode(encode(x)) == x`. When a property fails, Hypothesis shrinks the input to a small failing example, which is often the real lesson. If it fails on something you consider invalid input, tighten the strategy and write down the assumption. Good property candidates: round trips, idempotence, "output is never longer than input", and comparing a fast implementation to a simple one.
- Test Behavior, Not Implementation: Guiding Principles for UI Tests (https://testing-library.com/docs/guiding-principles/): Tests that break on every refactor teach teams to ignore them. The Testing Library project argues for tests that resemble how people use the software, because that is where confidence comes from.

Practical consequences, in any stack:
- Query elements the way a user finds them: by role, label or visible text, not by CSS class or internal component names.
- Assert on outcomes a user can see, such as a message appearing, not on state variables or method calls.
- Avoid testing private helpers directly. If a refactor changes internals but not behavior, the test should still pass.
- Mock at the network boundary, not inside your own modules.

A quick self-check for any test: if I rename an internal function, does it fail? If yes, it is coupled to implementation. If I break the feature, does it fail? If no, it is not protecting anything.

Use a few end-to-end tests for critical journeys and let faster, focused tests cover the rest.
- Broken Access Control: Stop Users Reading Each Other's Data (https://owasp.org/Top10/A01_2021-Broken_Access_Control/): In the 2021 edition of the OWASP Top 10 this category ranked first, and the common form is simple: change an id in a URL and see someone else's record.

``sql
-- vulnerable: trusts the id alone
SELECT * FROM invoices WHERE id = $1;

-- safer: ownership is part of the query
SELECT * FROM invoices WHERE id = $1 AND owner_id = $2;
`

Here $2` comes from the authenticated session, never from the request.

Habits that prevent most cases:
- Deny by default; require an explicit permission check on every endpoint.
- Enforce authorization on the server for every request. Hiding a button is not access control.
- Centralize checks in one policy layer instead of scattering ad hoc ifs.
- Prefer unguessable ids as defense in depth, not as the only defense.
- Write tests that log in as user A and request user B's resources, expecting 403 or 404.

Log denied attempts and alert on bursts of them.
- Challenge: Break and Fix a Query With SQL Injection (https://owasp.org/www-community/attacks/SQL_Injection): Run this on your own machine, in a throwaway file, to see the attack and the fix side by side. About ten minutes with Python.

``python
import sqlite3
db = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")
db.execute("create table users(name text, secret text)")
db.execute("insert into users values ('ana','a1'), ('bob','b2')")

name = "x' OR '1'='1"
bad = db.execute(f"select * from users where name = '{name}'").fetchall()
good = db.execute("select * from users where name = ?", (name,)).fetchall()
print(bad)   # every row leaks
print(good)  # []
``

The first query lets input rewrite the SQL. In the second, the driver sends the value separately from the statement, so it can only ever be data.

Your tasks:
1. Predict the output before running.
2. Find one place in a project of yours that builds SQL by concatenation and convert it.
3. Handle what placeholders cannot: table names, column names and ORDER BY direction. Check those against a fixed allowlist in code.

ORMs help but still allow raw string fragments, so review those too.
- IAM Least Privilege: Grant What the Job Needs, Nothing More (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/best-practices.html): Broad permissions turn a small leak into a big incident. The AWS IAM best-practices guide is worth reading even if you use another cloud, because the ideas transfer.

Core habits: prefer temporary credentials (roles) over long-lived access keys, require MFA for people, remove unused identities, and start narrow.

A scoped policy, read access to one prefix in one bucket:

``json
{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [{
    "Effect": "Allow",
    "Action": ["s3:GetObject"],
    "Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::my-bucket/reports/*"
  }]
}
``

How to get there in practice: begin with the smallest policy you can, test, and add what is denied. IAM Access Analyzer can help by generating a policy from recorded activity and by flagging resources shared outside your account. Remember that an explicit deny always wins over an allow, and avoid wildcards in both actions and resources unless you can justify them.

Review roles on a schedule; permissions only ever grow unless someone prunes them.
- Challenge: Audit Your Cloud Account for Public Storage (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/access-control-block-public-access.html): Accidentally public buckets are a classic cloud leak. Spend fifteen minutes checking an AWS account you own, using read-only commands. (Other clouds have equivalents; the habit is the point.)

``bash
aws s3api list-buckets --query 'Buckets[].Name' --output text
aws s3api get-public-access-block --bucket NAME
aws s3api get-bucket-policy-status --bucket NAME
`

How to read the results:
- get-public-access-block shows whether the four Block Public Access settings are on. An error saying no configuration exists means that bucket has none.
- get-bucket-policy-status reports IsPublic for the bucket policy.
- Also check the account-level setting with aws s3control get-public-access-block --account-id <id>`.

Your tasks: list every bucket that is not fully blocked, write down why each should be public (usually none should), and plan to enable Block Public Access at the account level. Serve public websites through a CDN instead of opening buckets. Do not change anything until you know which application depends on it.
- Debug Production With Logs, Metrics and Traces: Start With a Question (https://opentelemetry.io/docs/concepts/observability-primer/): Production debugging goes faster when you pick the right signal. Roughly: metrics say that something is wrong, traces say where in the request path, and logs say why.

A workable sequence:
1. State the symptom as a measurable question: "p95 latency of checkout rose after 14:00".
2. Use metrics to scope it: which service, endpoint, region, version?
3. Open a slow trace to find the span that takes the time.
4. Search logs for that request id to read the detail.

This only works if you prepared. Emit structured logs (JSON with fields) and include a request or trace id in every line, and pass it across service calls. Keep metric labels low-cardinality, so avoid user ids as labels.

Then form one hypothesis at a time and test it with a query, instead of changing things. The OpenTelemetry primer linked here explains the vocabulary of signals, context propagation and instrumentation clearly.
- Resume Basics: One Page That Survives a Quick Skim (https://www.techinterviewhandbook.org/resume/): A recruiter or engineer may spend under a minute on a first pass, so optimize for scanning.

Structure: contact line, short experience entries in reverse chronological order, projects, education, skills. Keep it to one page when you have under roughly a decade of experience.

Write each bullet as action, what you did, and the result:

``text
Weak:   Responsible for the billing service.
Better: Reduced invoice generation time by moving the job to a queue, cutting timeouts for large accounts.
``

Only use numbers you can defend in an interview; if you cannot measure it, describe the visible outcome honestly. Lead with the technologies that matter for the role, drop the ones you would not want to be quizzed on, and skip photos, rating bars and long objective statements.

Practical checks: export to PDF, make the text selectable, use a standard font, and ask a friend to circle the first three things they remember. Tailor the top third for each application.
- Behavioral Interviews: Build a Story Bank Before You Need It (https://www.techinterviewhandbook.org/behavioral-interview/): Behavioral questions test judgment and teamwork. Prepare, because improvised stories ramble.

A reliable shape is STAR: Situation, Task, Action, Result. Spend most of your time on Action and Result, and say "I" for what you did and "we" for what the team did.

Build a bank of four or five real stories from your work, studies or projects, and tag each with themes:
- a conflict or disagreement you worked through
- a failure and what changed afterward
- a tight deadline or trade-off
- leading or helping without authority
- something you learned quickly

Write each as bullet points, not a script, then practice aloud and time it to about two minutes. Prepare the follow-ups too: what would you do differently, and what did you measure?

Use only experiences that really happened. Interviewers probe details and inconsistencies show quickly. Finish with a result and a lesson, and close the loop if asked.
- Code Review That Helps: Habits for Authors and Reviewers (https://google.github.io/eng-practices/review/): Google's public engineering practices describe a simple standard: approve a change once it improves the overall health of the codebase, even if it is not how you would have written it. Perfect is not the bar.

For authors:
- Keep changes small and focused; they get reviewed faster and more carefully.
- Write a description that says what and why, and link the issue.
- Review your own diff first and run the tests.

For reviewers:
- Look at design, correctness, tests, naming and readability, roughly in that order of importance.
- Prefix minor preferences with "Nit:" so the author knows they are optional.
- Explain why, and ask questions before assuming a mistake.
- Respond promptly. Waiting for review is the biggest cost to the author.

Disagreement tip: when stuck in a loop, move to a call or a short design chat, then write the outcome in the thread. Comment on the code, never on the person.
- Write a Design Doc That Surfaces Trade-offs Early (https://www.industrialempathy.com/posts/design-docs-at-google/): A design doc is for finding problems while changes are still cheap. It is worth writing when a design is ambiguous or the choice involves real trade-offs, and not worth it when it would only describe obvious implementation.

A useful outline:
1. Context and scope: what this is and why now.
2. Goals and non-goals: non-goals prevent argument about things you never meant to solve.
3. The design: overview first, then APIs, data storage and key flows, with a diagram.
4. Alternatives considered, and why each lost.
5. Cross-cutting concerns: security, privacy, observability, rollout.

Keep it short for small work; a page or two is fine. Large projects naturally run longer, but split anything that sprawls.

Before sending, ask: could a reader tell what decision I want from them? Put that at the top, name reviewers, and set a date for comments. Record the final decision in the doc so it remains useful later.

### Open source worth reading
Awesome lists, starter templates and complete applications on GitHub, sorted by area. Reading real code is the fastest way to learn how projects are put together.
- awesome: the list that defines the format (https://github.com/sindresorhus/awesome): awesome is the meta-list behind the whole awesome-list convention, and it is the place to start when you want a curated index of anything from languages to tooling. Read create-list.md first: it explains what separates a useful list from link spam, which is handy if you ever curate one yourself. Then browse readme.md by topic. License: CC0-1.0, so you can reuse the material freely.
- awesome-selfhosted: services you can run yourself (https://github.com/awesome-selfhosted/awesome-selfhosted): A long, well-sorted catalogue of free software you can host on your own machines, grouped by what it replaces: wikis, monitoring, chat, media, backups and much more. Useful for homelab ideas and for finding a mature project to read. Start with README.md for the categories; non-free.md keeps proprietary entries separate so the main list stays clean. License: CC-BY-SA-3.0 for the list content.
- awesome-go: the Go ecosystem, categorised (https://github.com/avelino/awesome-go): If you write Go, this is the quickest way to find a library for routing, databases, CLIs, testing or concurrency without guessing. Entries are filtered for quality, so the list is shorter than a raw search. Fun extra: the repo ships its own Go code (main.go, pkg/, tmpl/) that builds the site, so you get a small real program to read too. License: MIT.
- awesome-ios: Swift and iOS libraries by topic (https://github.com/vsouza/awesome-ios): A large index of iOS and Swift projects grouped by purpose: networking, architecture, UI components, testing, tooling and learning material. Good when you need to compare two or three options before adding a dependency. Open README.md and use the table of contents; the architecture and testing sections are the most useful for people past their first app. License: MIT.
- magictools: a game developer's reference shelf (https://github.com/ellisonleao/magictools): One list that covers the practical side of making games: engines, art and audio tools, level editors, tutorials and communities. It is a good map if you are choosing a first engine or looking for free assets and tooling around it. Everything lives in README.md, organised by discipline, so skim the headings and jump to your area. License: MIT.
- awesome-machine-learning: libraries by language (https://github.com/josephmisiti/awesome-machine-learning): A language-by-language index of machine learning libraries, which makes it easy to see what exists in, say, Go or Rust and not only Python. Besides README.md, there are separate files for courses.md, books.md and ml-curriculum.md, handy for building a study plan. Treat it as a map and verify maintenance status before depending on any entry. License: CC0.
- kubernetes-the-hard-way: build a cluster by hand (https://github.com/kelseyhightower/kubernetes-the-hard-way): A classic tutorial that sets up Kubernetes step by step without installers, so you meet certificates, the API server, etcd and kubelet configuration directly. The numbered files in docs/ are the path; units/ and configs/ hold the files you generate or install. Not updated recently, but the concepts remain valid and the repo is still worth working through once. License: Apache-2.0.
- OWASP Cheat Sheet Series: concise security guidance (https://github.com/OWASP/CheatSheetSeries): Short, practical notes on how to build safely: authentication, session handling, input validation, secrets, REST security, Docker and many more. They are written for developers, not auditors. Browse the cheatsheets/ folder and start with Authentication_Cheat_Sheet.md, then read whatever matches your stack. Good to keep open during code review. License: CC BY-SA 4.0.
- LLMs-from-scratch: build a GPT-style model step by step (https://github.com/rasbt/LLMs-from-scratch): Code companion to a book on implementing a small language model in PyTorch, from tokenisation and attention to pretraining and fine-tuning. Chapters are folders, each with a 01_main-chapter-code directory; begin with ch03 for attention and ch04 for the full model. Bonus folders go deeper on topics such as KV cache and weight loading. License: Apache-2.0.
- ML-For-Beginners: a 12-week classical ML curriculum (https://github.com/microsoft/ML-For-Beginners): A lesson-based course built around classical machine learning: regression, classification, clustering, NLP and time series, with quizzes and notebooks. Each topic is a numbered folder, so you can read in order or jump in. 2-Regression is a gentle first stop, and 3-Web-App shows how to put a model behind a small app. License: MIT.
- rustlings: small exercises that teach Rust (https://github.com/rust-lang/rustlings): Tiny broken programs you fix until they compile, each one introducing a Rust idea such as ownership, enums or traits. It runs in your terminal and checks your work as you save. Look in exercises/ for the tasks and solutions/ once you are stuck. A fast way to get over the borrow checker's first hurdles. License: MIT.
- godot-demo-projects: small Godot games to read and run (https://github.com/godotengine/godot-demo-projects): Official demos that each isolate one feature of the Godot engine, so you can open a project and see exactly how it is wired. Browse 2d/, 3d/ and gui/, and read networking/ if you want multiplayer examples such as multiplayer_pong. Great for learning scenes, signals and GDScript by reading working code. License: MIT.
- full-stack-fastapi-template: a deployable API and UI (https://github.com/fastapi/full-stack-fastapi-template): A complete starting point pairing a FastAPI backend with a React frontend, PostgreSQL and Docker Compose. It is useful as a reference for auth, migrations, tests and deployment wiring. Open backend/ and frontend/ for the code, compose.yml to see the stack, then development.md and deployment.md for the workflow. License: MIT.
- create-t3-app: opinionated TypeScript web scaffolding (https://github.com/t3-oss/create-t3-app): A CLI that scaffolds a typed Next.js project, letting you opt into pieces like tRPC, Prisma or Drizzle and Tailwind. Reading cli/ shows how a good scaffolder composes templates and installers, which is a neat lesson on its own; www/ holds the documentation site. Use it when you want a well-trodden full-stack TypeScript layout. License: MIT.
- epic-stack: a full web app foundation with decisions explained (https://github.com/epicweb-dev/epic-stack): A production-minded starter for a React Router app with Prisma, Playwright tests and Fly.io deployment config. What sets it apart is documentation of why choices were made: read docs/ and the decisions folder inside it before the code. Then explore app/, prisma/ and tests/ to see how it all fits. License: MIT.
- awesome-compose: Docker Compose samples for common stacks (https://github.com/docker/awesome-compose): Ready-made Compose setups for pairings like Flask with Redis, Django, Nginx with Go and MySQL, Elasticsearch with Kibana, and more. Each sample is a folder with its own compose.yaml-style config, so you can copy only what you need. Handy for learning multi-container networking and volumes by running real examples. License: CC0-1.0.
- react-native-template-obytes: Expo app with good defaults (https://github.com/obytes/react-native-template-obytes): A mobile starter built on Expo and TypeScript with Maestro end-to-end flows in .maestro/, EAS build config in eas.json, and an organised src/ folder. Worth reading for how it sets up env handling, linting, commit hooks and tests so a team can start with discipline. License: MIT.
- chatbot: a Next.js AI chat app you can deploy (https://github.com/vercel/chatbot): A maintained reference for building a streaming chat product with the AI SDK, a database and authentication. Read app/ for routes, lib/ for data and model plumbing, artifacts/ for the artifacts feature, and tests/ for Playwright coverage. Good if you want to see how a modern AI app is structured end to end. License: Apache-2.0.
- cookiecutter-data-science: a sane layout for ML projects (https://github.com/drivendataorg/cookiecutter-data-science): A project template that gives data work a consistent structure for data, notebooks, source code and docs. The generated layout sits in the folder named {{ cookiecutter.repo_name }}, and ccds.json defines the prompts you answer. It also ships a Makefile with common tasks. A good habit-former for reproducible work. License: MIT.
- starter-workflows: GitHub Actions templates by use case (https://github.com/actions/starter-workflows): The official source of the workflow suggestions GitHub shows when you set up Actions. Folders like ci/, code-scanning/ and deployments/ hold YAML for building and testing many languages, scanning code and deploying to clouds. Read a few to learn caching, matrices and permissions idioms. License: MIT.
- architecture-samples: Android app structure, compared (https://github.com/android/architecture-samples): Google's reference to-do app showing how to structure an Android project with Compose, Hilt and Room. The main code is in app/ and shared test helpers live in shared-test/, so you can study the layers and how tests are organised. Pair it with Now in Android once the basics are comfortable. License: Apache-2.0.
- microservices-demo: Online Boutique on Kubernetes (https://github.com/GoogleCloudPlatform/microservices-demo): A polyglot web shop split into small services that talk over gRPC, designed to demonstrate cloud-native tooling. Start with kubernetes-manifests/ and skaffold.yaml to run it, then read service code under src/ and the API contracts in protos/. terraform/ and kustomize/ show alternative ways to deploy. License: Apache-2.0.
- excalidraw: a whiteboard app and an embeddable library (https://github.com/excalidraw/excalidraw): A real, widely used React app that is also published as a component. The editor lives in packages/excalidraw, the hosted app shell in excalidraw-app/, and dev-docs/ covers the internals and embedding. Study it for canvas rendering, state management and how a library is carved out of an app. License: MIT.
- Now in Android: a full modern Android reference (https://github.com/android/nowinandroid): A working news app that Google uses to demonstrate current Android practice: modular layout, Compose UI, offline-first data and thorough testing. Look at core/ and feature/ to see the module split, build-logic/ for convention plugins, and docs/ for architecture notes. Heavy but very instructive. License: Apache-2.0.
- Godot Engine: read a real game engine's source (https://github.com/godotengine/godot): A full 2D and 3D engine and editor in C++. Intimidating at first, but the layout helps: core/ holds fundamental types and the object system, scene/ the node tree, servers/ rendering and physics backends, and modules/ optional features. Pick one subsystem, such as input, and trace it through. License: MIT.
- Trivy: a vulnerability and misconfiguration scanner in Go (https://github.com/aquasecurity/trivy): A defensive scanner for container images, filesystems, IaC and dependencies. Reading it teaches how artifacts are unpacked and matched against advisories: pkg/fanal handles analysis of images and files, cmd/ wires the CLI, and docs/ explains usage. Run it against your own Dockerfile first. License: Apache-2.0.
- llama.cpp: LLM inference in plain C and C++ (https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp): A compact route to understanding how local language models actually run: quantised weights, a tensor library and efficient CPU and GPU backends. Read src/ for the model code, ggml/ for the tensor core, and convert_hf_to_gguf.py to see how models are converted. examples/ shows usage patterns. License: MIT.
- raylib: a friendly C library for making games (https://github.com/raysan5/raylib): A small, readable graphics and game library with a simple API and almost no dependencies. The examples/ folder is the best tutorial, with short programs covering 2D, 3D, audio and input, while src/ is approachable if you want to see how it works. CONVENTIONS.md documents the code style. License: zlib, a permissive one.
- age: a small, modern file encryption tool in Go (https://github.com/FiloSottile/age): A compact encryption library and CLI designed to be simple and hard to misuse. The core is a handful of readable files such as age.go, x25519.go and scrypt.go, with the command in cmd/ and extensibility in plugin/. A good example of a deliberately small cryptographic API. License: BSD-3-Clause.
- awesome-rust: where Rust projects are indexed (https://github.com/rust-unofficial/awesome-rust): A broad index of Rust libraries, applications and resources, organised by domain from web frameworks to embedded and games. Handy for discovering mature crates before you write your own. Open README.md, and see CONTRIBUTING.md if you want to add something. The repo also contains a small Rust crate (Cargo.toml, src/) alongside the list. License: CC0-1.0.
- awesome-docker: containers, tooling and learning resources (https://github.com/veggiemonk/awesome-docker): A curated map of the Docker ecosystem: tooling, security scanners, orchestration, CI helpers and tutorials. Read README.md by section when you hit a specific problem such as image size or registry choice. Alongside the list there is Go code in cmd/ and internal/, plus a website/ folder. License: Apache-2.0.
- awesome-android-ui: components worth studying (https://github.com/wasabeef/awesome-android-ui): A visual catalogue of Android UI libraries: animations, lists, dialogs, charts, transitions and more, with pointers to each repo. Useful when you want a polished interaction and would rather read an existing implementation. Everything is in README.md, and the art/ folder holds images. Check each library's maintenance before adopting. License: MIT.
- awesome-scalability: reading list for large-system design (https://github.com/binhnguyennus/awesome-scalability): A reading list of engineering write-ups on scalability, availability and stability, grouped by topic and by company. Good for getting beyond textbook diagrams to how real systems failed and recovered. Work through README.md one section at a time and note the trade-offs each article makes. License: MIT.
- TheAlgorithms/Python: algorithms with readable implementations (https://github.com/TheAlgorithms/Python): A large collection of algorithms and data structures written in plain Python for study. Folders such as dynamic_programming/, data_structures/, backtracking/ and ciphers/ make it easy to look up a topic, and DIRECTORY.md is the full index. Treat it as teaching code, not production code. License: MIT.
- ansible-for-devops: playbooks that grow with the book (https://github.com/geerlingguy/ansible-for-devops): Example playbooks from a well-known Ansible book, from simple to multi-server setups. Begin with first-ansible-playbook/, then lamp-infrastructure/, deployments-rolling/ and molecule/ for testing roles. The author notes that not every example follows every best practice, since each one illustrates a feature. Not updated every month, but the lessons last. License: MIT.
- generative-ai-for-beginners: lessons on building LLM apps (https://github.com/microsoft/generative-ai-for-beginners): A numbered course on building with large language models, covering prompts, text generation apps, chat, search, RAG and agents. Each lesson is a folder with explanations and code. Try 06-text-generation-apps, 15-rag-and-vector-databases and 17-ai-agents for practical angles. License: MIT.
- OWASP Web Security Testing Guide: a methodical checklist (https://github.com/OWASP/wstg): A defensive guide for testing web applications you own or are authorised to assess, organised by area such as authentication, session management and input handling. Use document/ for the chapters and checklists/ for working lists you can follow during a review. It also teaches developers what testers look for. License: CC BY-SA 4.0.
- micrograd: backpropagation in a few hundred lines (https://github.com/karpathy/micrograd): A tiny automatic-differentiation engine plus a small neural network library, built to show what frameworks do under the hood. Read micrograd/engine.py for the value graph and micrograd/nn.py for the layers, then run demo.ipynb. An evening's reading that makes training loops much less mysterious. License: MIT.
- mal: write a Lisp interpreter in small steps (https://github.com/kanaka/mal): A guided project to build a Lisp in numbered steps, with the same design implemented in dozens of languages under impls/. Start with process/guide.md, then compare your language's version with another you know. A rewarding way to learn parsing, evaluation, environments and tail calls. License: MPL-2.0.
- the-super-tiny-compiler: see a compiler in one file (https://github.com/jamiebuilds/the-super-tiny-compiler): A heavily commented JavaScript file that compiles a toy Lisp-like syntax into C-like calls, walking through tokenising, parsing, transforming and code generation. Read the-super-tiny-compiler.js top to bottom and run test.js. Older and small, but still a clear introduction to compiler stages. License: CC BY 4.0.
- openai-cookbook: worked examples for API-based apps (https://github.com/openai/openai-cookbook): A large set of notebooks and articles on building with LLM APIs: retrieval, function calling, evaluation, embeddings and more. Browse examples/ for runnable code and articles/ for longer guides. Treat the patterns as transferable even if you use another provider. License: MIT.
- handson-ml3: notebooks for classical and deep learning (https://github.com/ageron/handson-ml3): The code companion to a popular machine learning book, delivered as Jupyter notebooks that move from the basics to neural networks with Keras. Start with 02_end_to_end_machine_learning_project.ipynb for a full workflow, including data cleaning and evaluation. The notebooks explain choices as they go. License: Apache-2.0.
- OpenRCT2: a C++ game rebuilt and maintained in the open (https://github.com/OpenRCT2/OpenRCT2): An open-source reimplementation of a classic park simulation game. Because it models rides, guests, finances and a scenario world, it is a rich place to study simulation code. Start in src/openrct2, especially its world folder, and check docs/ for the build instructions. Original game data is needed to play. License: GPL-3.0.
- Mindustry: a complete Java game with desktop, Android and server (https://github.com/Anuken/Mindustry): A tower defence and factory game with its logic in core/, platform launchers in desktop/, android/ and ios/, and a headless server/ module. Reading it shows how one Java codebase targets many platforms with shared game code. CONTRIBUTING.md is the entry point for newcomers. License: GPL-3.0.
- opentelemetry-demo: a shop instrumented end to end (https://github.com/open-telemetry/opentelemetry-demo): A multi-language storefront built to show traces, metrics and logs in practice. Look through src/ to see the same telemetry ideas applied in different languages, and open compose.yaml for the local stack. A strong reference for observability wiring. License: Apache-2.0.
- Signal-Android: study a security-minded messenger (https://github.com/signalapp/Signal-Android): The Android client of a privacy-focused messenger, with a large modular Gradle layout (app/, lib/, core/) and a reproducible-builds/ folder explaining verifiable builds. Read it for encryption integration, background work and testing at scale. Heavy going, so pick one feature to trace. License: AGPL-3.0, which has strong copyleft terms.
- cal.diy: a scheduling app as a TypeScript monorepo (https://github.com/calcom/cal.diy): A large Next.js scheduling application organised into apps/ (including web, api and docs) and shared packages/ such as prisma, trpc and emails. Useful for seeing how a real product splits concerns across a monorepo. Check the README for how this repository relates to the hosted product. License: MIT.
- cookiecutter-django: production defaults for Django (https://github.com/cookiecutter/cookiecutter-django): A project generator that outputs a Django app with Docker, settings per environment, testing, and optional extras. Generate one, then read the template under {{cookiecutter.project_slug}} and the hooks/ that tailor the result. docs/ explains each option. License: BSD-3-Clause.
- Next-js-Boilerplate: a tidy starter with tests (https://github.com/ixartz/Next-js-Boilerplate): A Next.js and TypeScript starter that bundles Tailwind, a database layer with Drizzle, linting, Vitest and Playwright. See src/ for the app, migrations/ for schema history and tests/ for how the checks are organised. Handy when you want a starting point with quality gates already in place. License: MIT.
- ardanlabs/service: a layered Go service starter (https://github.com/ardanlabs/service): A reference layout for production Go web services with Kubernetes in mind. The structure is explicit: app/ for entry points, business/ for domain logic, foundation/ for reusable pieces, and zarf/ for deployment config. Good reading on package design and project layering. License: Apache-2.0.
- flutter/samples: small apps for each Flutter feature (https://github.com/flutter/samples): The Flutter team's collection of samples, each in its own folder: animations/, form_app/, compass_app/ and more. Pick one that matches the feature you need and read its code. compass_app/ is the one to study for app architecture. License: BSD-3-Clause.
- terraform-aws-vpc: a module worth copying habits from (https://github.com/terraform-aws-modules/terraform-aws-vpc): A widely used Terraform module for AWS networking. Read main.tf, variables.tf and outputs.tf for how a flexible module exposes options, then run the scenarios in examples/ and look at modules/. A good lesson in module design and interface choices. License: Apache-2.0.
- prisma-examples: ready-to-run TypeScript data layer samples (https://github.com/prisma/prisma-examples): A collection of example projects that pair Prisma with different frameworks and databases. Browse orm/ for framework samples, databases/ for database-specific setups and deployment-platforms/ for hosting. Note the default branch is called latest. License: Apache-2.0.
- podinfo: a small Go service for Kubernetes demos (https://github.com/stefanprodan/podinfo): A tiny web service used to try out deployment patterns. The repo includes Helm in charts/, plain manifests in kustomize/, a timoni/ module and signing config in .cosign/. Deploy it to learn rollout, health checks and supply-chain tooling. License: Apache-2.0.
- pydantic-ai: typed agents in Python (https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic-ai): An agent framework from the Pydantic team that leans on type hints for tools and structured outputs. Read pydantic_ai_slim/ for the core, pydantic_graph/ for graph-based control flow and pydantic_evals/ for evaluation, with examples/ to run. A good study in API design for LLM code. License: MIT.
- Bevy: a data-driven game engine in Rust (https://github.com/bevyengine/bevy): A modular engine built around an entity component system. The examples/ directory is organised by topic, and examples/ecs is the place to learn the core model, while crates/ shows how the engine is split. Fast-moving, so check the version when copying code. License: MIT or Apache-2.0.
- DuckDB: an analytical database you can read (https://github.com/duckdb/duckdb): An in-process SQL engine for analytics, written in C++. The src/ directory follows the query pipeline: parser, planner, optimizer, execution and storage. extension/ and benchmark/ are good side trips. A strong choice if you want to learn how databases work. License: MIT.
- OpenSSF Scorecard: automated checks on repo security habits (https://github.com/ossf/scorecard): A Go tool that scores open source projects on practices such as branch protection, dependency updates and pinned workflows. Read ARCHITECTURE.md, then look at checks/ and checks/raw/ to see how each check is implemented. Run it on your own repository. License: Apache-2.0.
- Falco: runtime threat detection for containers (https://github.com/falcosecurity/falco): A defensive runtime security tool that watches system activity and raises alerts based on rules. It is worth reading for how kernel events are turned into policy: see userspace/, then falco.yaml and config/ for configuration. Run it in a lab cluster to understand its output. License: Apache-2.0.

### Free ways to learn to code
Free courses, books, docs and practice sites, sorted by area and marked by level, so you can start where you are.
- CS50x (https://cs50.harvard.edu/x/): Harvard's free introduction to computer science. A demanding and very well-taught foundation for any track.
- freeCodeCamp (https://www.freecodecamp.org/): A free interactive curriculum with projects and certifications, covering web development, Python, data and more.
- The Odin Project (https://www.theodinproject.com/): A free, project-based full-stack web curriculum that teaches you to use real tools from the start.
- Full Stack Open (https://fullstackopen.com/en/): The University of Helsinki's free course on modern web development with React, Node.js and testing.
- The Missing Semester of Your CS Education (https://missing.csail.mit.edu/): MIT lectures on the tools most courses skip: the shell, editors, Git, debugging and more.
- Practical Deep Learning for Coders (https://course.fast.ai/): fast.ai's free course teaches deep learning by building working models first and explaining the theory after.
- Kaggle Learn (https://www.kaggle.com/learn): Short, free, hands-on micro-courses on Python, pandas, SQL and machine learning that run in the browser.
- Android Basics with Compose (https://developer.android.com/courses/android-basics-compose/course): Google's free course for building Android apps with Kotlin and Jetpack Compose, with no experience needed.
- OWASP Cheat Sheet Series (https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/): Concise, practical guidance on specific application security topics such as authentication and input validation.
- Devhints (https://devhints.io/): A big collection of short, readable cheatsheets for languages, frameworks and command-line tools.
- tldr pages (https://tldr.sh/): Community-written command-line help with practical examples, instead of long man pages.
- GitHub Git Cheat Sheet (https://education.github.com/git-cheat-sheet-education.pdf): A one-page PDF of the Git commands you will use every day.
- roadmap.sh (https://roadmap.sh/): Community-built learning roadmaps and guides for almost every developer role.
- MDN: Learn web development (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Learn_web_development): Mozilla's structured path through HTML, CSS and JavaScript, from one of the web's most trusted references.
- web.dev Learn (https://web.dev/learn): Free courses from Chrome's developer relations team on CSS, performance, accessibility and more.
- The Twelve-Factor App (https://12factor.net/): A short, influential guide to building services that are easy to deploy, configure and scale.
- Learn OpenGL (https://learnopengl.com/): A free, thorough guide to modern graphics programming, from your first triangle to advanced lighting.
- Site Reliability Engineering (https://sre.google/sre-book/table-of-contents/): Google's book on running production systems, free to read online.
- Pro Git (https://git-scm.com/book/en/v2): The complete Git book, free to read online, from the basics to how Git works internally.
- Eloquent JavaScript (https://eloquentjavascript.net/): A well-loved book on JavaScript and programming in general, free to read online.
- The Rust Programming Language (https://doc.rust-lang.org/book/): The official Rust book, free online. A clear introduction to ownership and systems programming.
- The Swift Programming Language (https://docs.swift.org/swift-book/): The official guide to Swift, free online. The language behind modern iOS development.
- Docker: Get started (https://docs.docker.com/get-started/): The official hands-on introduction to containers, images and Compose.
- Kubernetes Basics (https://kubernetes.io/docs/tutorials/kubernetes-basics/): The official interactive tutorial for deploying, scaling and updating an app on Kubernetes.
- The Python Tutorial (https://docs.python.org/3/tutorial/): The official Python tutorial. A clear tour of the language for people who have programmed a little.
- Flutter documentation (https://docs.flutter.dev/): Official docs and learning paths for building iOS, Android, web and desktop apps from one codebase.
- Godot documentation (https://docs.godotengine.org/en/stable/): Official docs for the free, open-source Godot engine, including step-by-step first game tutorials.
- Learn Git Branching (https://learngitbranching.js.org/): An interactive, visual way to learn branching and rebasing right in your browser.
- SQLBolt (https://sqlbolt.com/): Short interactive lessons that teach SQL by writing real queries in the browser.
- A Tour of Go (https://go.dev/tour/): The official interactive introduction to Go. You run every example in the browser.
- Web Security Academy (https://portswigger.net/web-security): Free, legal labs from PortSwigger that teach real web vulnerabilities and how to prevent them.
- OverTheWire Wargames (https://overthewire.org/wargames/): Legal hacking games that teach Linux and security concepts. Start with Bandit.
- freeCodeCamp on YouTube (https://www.youtube.com/c/Freecodecamp): Thousands of hours of free full-length programming courses on nearly every topic.

### Tools developers keep
Command-line tools, frameworks and libraries that save time every week, from Kubernetes dashboards to infrastructure as code.
- OpenTofu (https://opentofu.org/): An open-source, community-driven infrastructure-as-code tool that is a fork of Terraform.
- Ansible (https://docs.ansible.com/): Agentless automation for configuring servers and deploying software using readable YAML playbooks.
- Prometheus (https://prometheus.io/): A widely used open-source monitoring system and time-series database with its own query language.
- Grafana (https://grafana.com/oss/grafana/): Open-source dashboards for your metrics, logs and traces from many data sources.
- Trivy (https://trivy.dev/): An open-source scanner for vulnerabilities and misconfigurations in containers, code and infrastructure.
- FastAPI (https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/): A modern Python web framework that uses type hints for validation and automatic API docs.
- PostgreSQL (https://www.postgresql.org/): A powerful open-source relational database and a safe default for most applications.
- Vite (https://vite.dev/): A fast frontend build tool and dev server with instant updates as you edit.
- Playwright (https://playwright.dev/): Reliable end-to-end browser testing across Chromium, Firefox and WebKit.
- scikit-learn (https://scikit-learn.org/): The standard Python library for classic machine learning, with excellent documentation.
- Hugging Face Transformers (https://github.com/huggingface/transformers): An open-source library for using and training state-of-the-art machine learning models.
- Flutter (https://flutter.dev/): Google's open-source UI toolkit for building mobile, web and desktop apps from a single codebase.
- Tauri (https://tauri.app/): Build small, secure desktop and mobile apps with a web frontend and a Rust backend.
- Godot Engine (https://godotengine.org/): A free and open-source 2D and 3D game engine with no royalties.
- ripgrep (https://github.com/BurntSushi/ripgrep): An extremely fast tool for searching code that respects your .gitignore by default.
- jq (https://jqlang.org/): A small command-line tool for slicing, filtering and transforming JSON.
- k9s (https://k9scli.io/): A terminal UI for managing Kubernetes clusters. It makes it much faster to inspect pods, read logs and jump between resources than typing kubectl commands.
- lazygit (https://github.com/jesseduffield/lazygit): A simple terminal UI for Git. Staging single lines, rebasing and resolving conflicts all become much easier to see and do.
- ShellCheck (https://www.shellcheck.net/): A linter that finds bugs in shell scripts, such as unquoted variables. Try it in the browser or add it to your CI.
- Caddy (https://caddyserver.com/): A web server and reverse proxy that gets and renews HTTPS certificates automatically, with very little configuration.
- fzf (https://github.com/junegunn/fzf): A general-purpose fuzzy finder for the command line. Use it to search files, shell history, Git branches and anything else you can pipe into it.
- Gitleaks (https://github.com/gitleaks/gitleaks): Finds passwords, API keys and tokens in your Git history. Run it as a pre-commit hook or in CI before a secret gets out.
- DuckDB (https://duckdb.org/): An in-process analytical database. Query CSV and Parquet files with SQL on your laptop, with no server to run.
- pre-commit (https://pre-commit.com/): A framework for managing Git hooks, so linters and formatters run automatically before every commit.
- hadolint (https://github.com/hadolint/hadolint): A Dockerfile linter that catches bad practices and checks the shell code inside your RUN instructions.
- Bruno (https://www.usebruno.com/): An open-source API client that stores your collections as plain files, so they can live in Git with your code.
- dive (https://github.com/wagoodman/dive): Explore each layer of a Docker image and find wasted space, so you can make your images smaller.
- htmx (https://htmx.org/): A small library that adds dynamic behaviour with HTML attributes. Build interactive pages without a large frontend framework.
- Semgrep (https://github.com/semgrep/semgrep): Fast static analysis for many languages, with rules that look like the code you are searching for.
- act (https://github.com/nektos/act): Run your GitHub Actions workflows locally to test changes without pushing a commit every time.
- SQLite (https://www.sqlite.org/): A small, reliable database stored in a single file, with no server required. It is often all a small project needs.
- bat (https://github.com/sharkdp/bat): A cat replacement with syntax highlighting, line numbers and Git integration.
- Uptime Kuma (https://github.com/louislam/uptime-kuma): A self-hosted monitoring tool with a clean dashboard, status pages and many notification options.
- MkDocs (https://www.mkdocs.org/): Turn a folder of Markdown files into a clean documentation site, with very little setup.
- ZAP (https://www.zaproxy.org/): A free, open-source web application security scanner. Only use it against applications you own or have permission to test.
- Hoppscotch (https://hoppscotch.io/): A lightweight, open-source API testing tool that runs in your browser and can also be self-hosted.
- Valkey (https://valkey.io/): An open-source, high-performance key-value datastore, forked from Redis and backed by the Linux Foundation.
- tmux (https://github.com/tmux/tmux): A terminal multiplexer. Split your terminal into panes and keep sessions running after you disconnect from a server.
- Renovate (https://github.com/renovatebot/renovate): Automates dependency updates by opening pull requests, so your projects do not silently fall behind.
- Wireshark (https://www.wireshark.org/): The classic network protocol analyzer. See exactly what is on the wire when something will not connect.
- Excalidraw (https://excalidraw.com/): A free, open-source whiteboard with a hand-drawn style. It is great for quick architecture diagrams.
- HTTPie (https://github.com/httpie/cli): A friendly command-line HTTP client with readable syntax and formatted output, made for working with APIs.

## Tips
- git commit --amend changes your most recent commit. Avoid amending a commit you have already pushed to a shared branch, because it rewrites history.
- Use git switch -c new-branch to create a branch and move to it in one step.
- git stash sets aside your uncommitted changes so you can switch tasks. git stash pop brings them back.
- Lost a commit? git reflog lists where HEAD has been recently, so you can usually get it back.
- git bisect uses a binary search through your history to find the commit that introduced a bug.
- git log --oneline --graph --all gives you a quick visual map of your branches.
- git diff --staged shows exactly what your next commit will contain.
- git add -p lets you stage parts of a file, which helps keep each commit focused on one change.
- Write commit messages that explain why a change was made. The diff already shows what changed.
- Keep secrets out of Git. If one is ever committed, assume it is compromised and revoke it, even after you delete it from history.
- Add a .gitignore before your first commit so build output and .env files never get tracked.
- In the shell, Ctrl+R searches your command history. It saves a lot of retyping.
- !! in Bash repeats your last command. sudo !! reruns it with sudo.
- Quote your shell variables: "$file" rather than $file. Unquoted variables break on spaces.
- Start Bash scripts with set -euo pipefail so they stop on errors, unset variables and failed pipes.
- curl -I https://example.com fetches only the response headers, which is handy for checking redirects and caching.
- ss -tulpn shows which processes are listening on which ports on Linux. It replaces the older netstat.
- du -sh * | sort -h shows what is using disk space in the current folder, sorted by size.
- tail -f app.log follows a log file live. journalctl -u myservice -f does the same for a systemd service.
- chmod 777 is rarely the right fix. Find out which user needs access and give only that user what it needs.
- Use SSH keys rather than passwords for your servers, then disable password login.
- In Docker, copy your dependency manifest and install before you copy your source code. Layer caching will make rebuilds much faster.
- Multi-stage Docker builds keep compilers and build tools out of your final image, so it is smaller and has less to attack.
- Do not run containers as root unless you must. Add a USER instruction to your Dockerfile.
- Pin your base images to a specific version. latest can change under you and break a build with no code change.
- Add a .dockerignore file so node_modules, .git and secrets do not end up in your build context.
- docker system df shows how much space images, containers and volumes use. docker system prune removes unused data, so read its warning first.
- In Kubernetes, set resource requests and limits on your containers so one workload cannot starve the others.
- A liveness probe restarts a stuck container. A readiness probe stops traffic until the container is ready. They solve different problems.
- kubectl describe pod <name> is usually the first step in debugging. Its Events section often tells you exactly what went wrong.
- Make your CI fail fast: run linting and unit tests before slower integration tests and builds.
- Treat your infrastructure like code: keep it in version control and review changes like any other pull request.
- Deploys should be boring. Small, frequent releases are easier to review, debug and roll back than big ones.
- Practice restoring your backups. A backup you have never restored is only a hope.
- Alert on symptoms users feel, like errors and slow responses, rather than on every internal metric.
- Structured logs (such as JSON) are far easier to search and filter than free-form text.
- Log enough to debug a problem, but never log passwords, tokens or personal data.
- Always use parameterized queries for SQL. Building queries by joining strings invites SQL injection.
- Store passwords with a slow password hash such as Argon2 or bcrypt. Never store them in plain text, and do not use a fast hash like MD5 or SHA-256 alone.
- Validate input on the server, even if you already validate it in the browser. Client-side checks can be bypassed.
- Run npm audit, pip-audit or your language's equivalent regularly to find dependencies with known vulnerabilities.
- Add an index for columns you filter on often, and use EXPLAIN to confirm your query actually uses it.
- An N+1 query problem happens when you run one query per row in a loop. Fetch the related data in one query instead.
- Wrap related database writes in a transaction, so they either all succeed or all fail together.
- Use <button> for actions and <a> for navigation. You get keyboard support and accessibility for free.
- Every meaningful image needs useful alt text. Purely decorative images should use an empty alt="".
- CSS gap works with both flexbox and grid. It is often simpler than adding margins to each child.
- Open the browser's Network tab before guessing. It shows the exact request, response and timing.
- Use const by default in JavaScript. Use let only when a value really needs to change.
- await in a loop runs tasks one at a time. Use Promise.all when they can safely run at the same time.
- In Python, use a virtual environment per project: python -m venv .venv. It keeps dependencies from clashing.
- In Python, avoid a mutable default argument such as def f(items=[]). The same list is shared across calls. Use None instead.
- Read the whole error message from the top, especially the first line that mentions your code. It usually says more than it first seems.
- When you are stuck, write the smallest example that reproduces the bug. You will often find the cause while doing it.
- Explain your bug out loud to someone, or to a rubber duck. Saying it step by step often exposes the wrong assumption.
- Change one thing at a time when debugging. If you change five things, you will not know which one mattered.
- A failing test is the best way to start fixing a bug. It proves the bug exists and shows when it is gone.
- Test behaviour rather than implementation details, so your tests still pass when you refactor.
- Name things for what they mean, not how they work. Good names can replace a lot of comments.
- Comments should explain why the code does something surprising. The code itself should show what it does.
- Read other people's code. Picking one open-source project and following how it works teaches things tutorials cannot.
- Take breaks. Many hard bugs get solved on a walk, once your brain stops repeating the same wrong idea.
